title: Dumfries: Mourinho and I still talk about Inter, one player ‘tells me everything’
description: Denzel Dumfries admits he and José Mourinho still talk about Inter and follow the Nerazzurri, and reveals: ‘I talk a lot with Marcus [Thuram], and we still make the same jokes about each other, and...
fullText:
Denzel Dumfries admits he and José Mourinho still talk about Inter and follow the Nerazzurri, and reveals: 'I talk a lot with Marcus [Thuram], and we still make the same jokes about each other, and he tells me everything.'

Dumfries joined Real Madrid from Inter last summer.

The Merengues activated the Dutchman's €20m release clause to take him from the Nerazzurri after five years.

At the Bernabéu, Dumfries reunited with a legendary former Inter coach, Mourinho.

HOUSTON, TEXAS – JUNE 20: Denzel Dumfries #22 of Netherlands arrives at the stadium before the FIFA World Cup 2026 Group F match between Netherlands and Sweden at Houston Stadium on June 20, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Molly Darlington/Getty Images)

"I like him a lot; he's a great coach. Just look at what he's done in his career. Of course, I know about his past at Inter, too," Dumfries told Libero.

"We're just at the beginning of the season, and we're starting to get to know each other, but the first signs are very good.

"We've talked a lot about Inter. The time we spent there was very special for both of us. We love Inter; we keep following them, and we talk about it.

"I follow everything, and I still talk to my former teammates. It's normal," he continued.

"I talk a lot with Marcus [Thuram], and we still make the same jokes about each other, and he tells me everything. Over these five years, we became a family. Now I follow them from afar, but I see everything."

MILAN, ITALY – APRIL 21: Marcus Thuram and Denzel Dumfries of FC Internazionale Milano celebrate after the Coppa Italia Semi-Final match between FC Internazionale and Como at San Siro on April 21, 2026 in Milan, Italy. (Photo by Marco Luzzani/Getty Images)

When asked to name those he got along with best at Inter, the Netherlands international replied with a smile: "I don't want to make anyone angry! Definitely Marcus, Bisseck, Hakan [Calhanoglu], Akanji, de Vrij and Onana."

Inter, Dumfries and Mourinho have already reunited this season, meeting in the Champions League round 1 at the Bernabéu.

"When I saw that we were going to play against Inter, it was great," Dumfries said.

"At first, I even thought we were going to play at San Siro. I texted the guys saying: 'I know all your tactics, you won't be able to surprise me!' And they joked back that they were going to play 4-4-2, so I wouldn't know what to expect.

"It was really nice, although obviously a little strange. Before and after the match it was very special; during the game, though… It's business, and you have to compete against each other."

MADRID, SPAIN – SEPTEMBER 08: Jose Mourinho, Head Coach of Real Madrid looks on before the UEFA Champions League 2026/27 League Phase MD1 match between Real Madrid C.F. and FC Internazionale Milano at Estadio Santiago Bernabeu on September 08, 2026 in Madrid, Spain. (Photo by Denis Doyle/Getty Images)

Dumfries has only just started his career at Real Madrid, but is already enjoying the Spanish capital, on and off the pitch.

"I really like it. It's such a beautiful city, and I'm really happy," he said.

"Obviously, it's difficult to find a better place than Milan, so I had to be careful picking the new city and the new club. I'm really happy.

"After five years at Inter, I felt that it was the right time to try something new. To me, Real Madrid are the biggest club in the world, and it's a privilege to play here. It had nothing to do with Inter because I had an incredible time there.

"After the [2025-26] season ended, before the World Cup, my agent called to say he was in contact with Real Madrid. I was happy and proud.

"I immediately told Piero [Ausilio]. I had a great relationship with him and everyone at Inter, and I wanted them to know right away."

CAGLIARI, ITALY – AUGUST 28: Piero Ausilio sporting director of Inter looks on during the Serie A TIM match between Cagliari Calcio and FC Internazionale at Sardegna Arena on August 28, 2023 in Cagliari, Italy. (Photo by Enrico Locci/Getty Images)

Dumfries was on excellent terms with both Ausilio, who has now left Inter, and the Nerazzurri president Giuseppe Marotta.

"To me, they are great people," Dumfries said.

"Even when it came time to discuss my contract, we were always honest with each other. I considered my age, my goals, and my career. We always spoke openly. Having this kind of relationship with my sporting director was very important. We did everything the right way. They were five special years."

Last but not least, Dumfries spoke about his favourite moments at Inter.

"I'd say the first Scudetto. The last one was also very special, but the first was incredible," he concluded.

"The second star is something that will remain in history forever. Of course, the last Scudetto was a huge surprise. Everyone was looking at Inter and wondering what would happen. Winning the double with Chivu was fantastic. They were incredible years."

title: Phillies’ Alec Bohm Sends Front Office Message After Brutal Exit
description: The Philadelphia Phillies polarizing former All-Star offered a clear response for president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski.
fullText:
The Philadelphia Phillies entered the postseason hoping to extend a competitive window that has already produced some deep October runs, but their latest opportunity ended abruptly against a familiar division rival.

The Atlanta Braves eliminated the Phillies with a blowout victory in Game 3 of the National League Wild Card Series, sending the Braves to a Division Series matchup with the reigning World Series champions.

"It will be the NL East champion Atlanta facing the NL West champion Los Angeles Dodgers in the NL Division Series," USA Today's Bob Nightengale reported. "Atlanta eliminates Philadelphia, 6-2."

The loss also brought an important question into focus for Alec Bohm, whose future in the sport remains uncertain. After the final game, the impending free agent made clear that he would like to remain with the organization.

"I definitely feel like we have unfinished business here, and I want to be a part of the team that gets it done, for sure," Bohm said, according to Phillies Nation's Ty Daubert.

Dodgers' Kyle Tucker Responds To Contract Disappointment, 'I Don't Really Care'

Bohm's Phillies career has included considerable highs and lows since Philadelphia selected him third overall in the 2018 MLB Draft. He became an All-Star in 2024, but inconsistent production and repeated questions about his place on the roster have made him a central figure in trade rumors.

This season, the Phillies changed his defensive role after acquiring Luis Arraez at the trade deadline, moving Bohm from third base to first base as the club adjusted its alignment. That move was part of another roller coaster campaign for Bohm, which saw a brutal start turn into a productive finish at the plate.

"Bohm's Phillies career has been sometimes frustrating, sometimes exciting, sometimes perplexing," Charlotte Varnes noted for The Athletic. "But the best adjective to describe Bohm's 2026 is tumultuous."

Cubs' 6-Year Infielder, Historic Franchise First, Dies After Pioneering Career

Bohm's comments came after he delivered one of the biggest moments of Philadelphia's postseason run. He hit the go-ahead home run in the 10th inning of Game 2 against Atlanta, helping the Phillies force a decisive third game. That performance gave him another opportunity to influence the club's postseason fate after a season filled with questions about his future.

His desire to stay also comes after months of uncertainty surrounding whether the Phillies would look to keep him around into the future. Allowing him to sign a contract with a new team could be one of the easiest ways to adjust a roster that appears to be in need of an overhaul.

For now, there is no indication that Philadelphia has made a decision on Bohm's future. His final message, however, was unmistakable: after a notable run with the Phillies, he wants the chance to keep building his career in the same place.

This article was originally published on Forbes.com

title: Why Bahrain is Paying Millions to Rent Malaysia’s Sepang Circuit for the 2026 F1 Season
description: If you glance at the timing screens for this weekend’s Formula 1 action, you might do a double-take. The paddock has set up camp at the iconic Sepang International Circuit in Selangor, Malaysia, yet the official event title is the…
fullText:
If you glance at the timing screens for this weekend's Formula 1 action, you might do a double-take. The paddock has set up camp at the iconic Sepang International Circuit in Selangor, Malaysia, yet the official event title is the "Formula 1 Gulf Air Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia 2026″.

It is one of the most unprecedented logistical and financial pivots in modern motorsport history. Instead of simply canceling the race and taking a massive financial hit, the Kingdom of Bahrain opted to effectively rent an entire country's racetrack, packing up its Grand Prix and moving it 6,000 kilometers east.

Here is exactly why Bahrain is paying top dollar to host its own home race in the Malaysian jungle.

The Bahrain Grand Prix was originally scheduled to be the fourth round of the 2026 World Championship, slated for the weekend of April 10–12 at the Bahrain International Circuit in Sakhir.

However, on February 28, 2026, the outbreak of the Iran war drastically altered the global sporting landscape. Following targeted airstrikes by the United States and Israel, Iran launched counterattacks against numerous American military bases across the Middle East, including facilities located in Bahrain. By March 14, Formula 1 and the FIA officially called off both the Bahrain and Saudi Arabian Grands Prix due to severe safety concerns.

Losing two highly lucrative Middle Eastern markets was a massive blow to F1's revenue streams. But while Saudi Arabia's race was permanently scrapped from the 2026 calendar, Bahrain's promoters refused to let their event die.

Bahrain currently holds an ironclad contract to remain on the Formula 1 calendar until 2036. Rather than breach that contract or lose out on the massive global exposure of an F1 weekend, Bahrain's Crown Prince and Prime Minister, Salman bin Hamad Al Khalifa, orchestrated a radical alternative to show the country's "commitment to, and passion for (F1)".

Under a landmark agreement between F1, the FIA, and the Malaysian government, the race was relocated to Sepang in early October, slotting perfectly between the Azerbaijan and Singapore Grands Prix.

KUALA LUMPUR, MALAYSIA – OCTOBER 03: Max Verstappen of the Netherlands and Oracle Red Bull Racing and Isack Hadjar of France and Oracle Red Bull Racing on the fan stage prior to final practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Bahrain in Malaysia at Sepang Circuit on October 03, 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. (Photo by Sona Maleterova/Getty Images) // Getty Images / Red Bull Content Pool // SI202610030108 // Usage for editorial use only //

Crucially, this is not a Malaysian Grand Prix funded by Kuala Lumpur. Bahrain is entirely footing the bill for the relocation and the massive operational costs of staging the race at Sepang. In exchange for fully financing the event, the Bahraini organizers retain complete ownership of the Grand Prix's identity, as well as 100% of the ticket pricing rights and race proceeds.

For Malaysia, it's a win-win. Sepang gets to host its first Formula 1 race since 2017 without paying F1's exorbitant multi-million-dollar hosting fees. They are simply acting as a venue supplier for Bahrain's production.

Because Bahrain owns the financial rights to the weekend, they have gone all out to ensure the event still feels like a Middle Eastern spectacle despite the tropical setting.

The organization from Bahrain flew its own staff from the Bahrain International Circuit directly to Malaysia to run the event. They are actively providing the catering, the facilities, and the VIP entertainment.

Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, Friday KUALA LUMPUR, MALAYSIA – OCTOBER 02: Andrea Kimi Antonelli of Italy driving the (12) Mercedes AMG Petronas F1 Team W17 leads George Russell of Great Britain driving the (63) Mercedes AMG Petronas F1 Team W17 on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Bahrain in Malaysia at Sepang Circuit on October 02, 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. (Photo by Sam Bloxham/LAT Images)

Fans walking around the Sepang paddock are completely immersed in Bahraini culture. The fan zone has been transformed into a "Bahrain Village," featuring authentic Middle Eastern music, crafts, and cuisine. Even the familiar paddock setups and traditional Bahraini podium ceremonies have been imported directly to Southeast Asia.

It is an incredibly bizarre sight for long-time F1 fans, but the unusual "Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia" name is entirely accurate. Bahrain didn't just sponsor a race—they literally bought a weekend on Malaysian soil to keep their Formula 1 dreams alive.

title: Skip Bayless tells Stephen A. Smith his top five NFL quarterbacks right now
description: Skip Bayless made an appearance on one of Stephen A. Smith’s YouTube channels this week and was quizzed on the top quarterbacks in the NFL this season.
fullText:
Skip Bayless made an appearance on one of Stephen A. Smith's YouTube channels this week and was quizzed on the top quarterbacks in the NFL this season.

The 2026/27 season is only a few games old, but there are already some standout teams emerging, including the Kansas City Chiefs.

And while he did initially forget about the Chiefs star, Patrick Mahomes was named as one of the top five quarterbacks by Bayless.

After some back-and-forth, Skip decided his top five is: Patrick Mahomes, Brock Purdy, Josh Allen, Lamar Jackson, and Joe Burrow, putting Dak Prescott in sixth place.

Bayless initially explained: "Brock Purdy is up there because he's playing at the highest level without his two, without Stribling and Pearsall, and now it sounds like no Mike Evans. So he's number one in QBR.

"I still think Joe Burrow is way up there. Lamar is still up there. Obviously, Josh Allen is way up there. I don't like the five-turnover game, but he's way up there.

"So, did I get to five yet or am I at four? Um, who am I forgetting? Um, I'll put Dak up there. I think Dak has played at an extremely high, just-throwing-the-football level.

Smith then replied: "Yeah. So, right now, you're talking about Patrick Mahomes, you're talking about Lamar Jackson…"

Bayless then remembered: "I left out Patrick Mahomes. That's who should be in the top five. Yes."

Smith then clarified: "Alright. So, Patrick Mahomes, Brock Purdy, Josh Allen, Lamar Jackson, and Dak Prescott?"

To which Bayless responded: "No, I'll take Joe before Dak. I'll say Dak is sixth."

At the time of writing, the NFL have Purdy sitting top of their quarterback rankings.

Mahomes, who of course returned from his injury this season, takes second place.

title: Amarius Mims draws strong praise from offensive line guru
description: The Bengals once again have a dominant right tackle.
fullText:
If there was a true bright spot that has been consistent throughout the season so far for the Cincinnati Bengals, it would be right tackle Amarius Mims playing practically perfect.

Mims has shut down every pass rusher he has gone against so far. That list includes the likes of Will Anderson Jr. and Danielle Hunter from the Houston Texans.

It also includes T.J. Watt from the game on Sunday with the Pittsburgh Steelers. That performance caught the eye of Brandon Thorn — one of the best offensive linemen evaluators — who has high praise after Mims incredible start, calling him a top 5-to-6 right tackle in the NFL.

Counted 12 true drop-back, 1v1 reps from Mims vs. Watt, who was shut down working high-side, down the middle and inside. This is a top 5-6 RT in just his 3rd season 📈📈📈 pic.twitter.com/AVGY5fApQ6

"This is a top 5-6 RT in just his 3rd season," said Thorn.

The knock on Mims during the draft process was that he couldn't stay healthy. That always seemed unfounded considering he never even had a major knee injury. Just some moderate to minor injuries that popped up near the end of his time in college and during the draft process itself. It also created a lack-of-experience concern, but he never had an issue in the SEC.

That's why the Bengals may have gotten the steal of the draft at No. 18 overall in the 2024 NFL Draft. He has hit what many called his high ceiling of potential. Those kinds of picks haven't always worked out, but it is clear they nailed this one if Mims can stay healthy.

The only question that comes now is if he eventually gets moved to left tackle. Orlando Brown Jr. has struggled a bit with some of the quicker rushers in the NFL, and it has showed up quite a few times over the years, but he is far from being an unacceptable starter. It may come down to whether they feel the move can be made, and how much exactly they end up having to pay him when that contract needs to be redone. Because he surely should push for elite tackle money, but left tackle will always get 

That is a long-term discussion, though. We get to enjoy him as an absolute dominant offensive tackle right now.

title: Burrillville football steamrolls Woonsocket as running game steals show
description: Marcoccio received the bulk of the carries in place of fellow senior Caden Hebert (undisclosed injury), who sat this one out along with other regulars
fullText:
WOONSOCKET – The program's storied football history being what it is, it would still be difficult to imagine too many Burrillville running backs ever enjoying a night like this one.

Joey Marcoccio turned Dionne Track into his own personal playground, and the Broncos trampled a regional rival in what was billed coming in as a Division II showdown.

Marcoccio exploded for 294 yards on the ground and three touchdowns as Burrillville imposed its will up front all night. Woonsocket was powerless to stop the onslaught, as the Broncos steamed their way to a 41-18 triumph under the lights.

More: Rhode Island high school football Week 4 schedules, scores and stats

The threatening pregame clouds largely held their precipitation as they moved through the area – Marcoccio took it upon himself to open the floodgates. He cracked the 100-yard mark by halftime and was already over the 200-yard threshhold when he finished a hat trick with 11:17 left, a spectacular 90-yard scoring rush up the middle and toward the right sideline.

"I just had it," Marcoccio said. "I was visualizing it. I was trying to get it in my mind and visualizing these blocks.

"We had a great game plan. We have great (offensive) linemen. They did their jobs."

Burrillville effectively put this one out of reach early in the third quarter, following a statement drive with a turnover and a second score. Marcoccio capped a 10-play march that chewed up 7:24 on the clock when he zipped through the right side from 4 yards out to make it 27-6. Jackson Deschamps came up with a fumble recovery on the first Villa Novan play after the change of possession and Marcoccio raced 29 yards around the left side to open a 34-6 cushion with 3:12 to play.

"Monday during our walkthrough Coach (Gennaro) Ferraro was like, 'This is Joey's week. He's going to come out. He's going to have a game,'" Burrillville quarterback Chace Gavis said. "We've been waiting on it."

The Broncos might have planned to run some clock after Jalil Quinones Diaz twisted and powered his way to a 24-yard touchdown run with 11:39 left in the fourth, but Marcoccio wasn't having it. He took a handoff up the middle on the first Burrillville play of the ensuing possession and was off, streaking between defensive backs down the middle. He cut toward the right sideline and had just enough juice left to crack the goal line, a third scoring rush on what was a career evening.

"I was exhausted," Marcoccio said. "I started cramping up at the end. I was like, 'I see this end zone – I'm not going to give up now.'"

Marcoccio received the bulk of the carries in place of fellow senior Caden Hebert (undisclosed injury), who sat this one out along with multiple Broncos regulars. The converted wide receiver combined the quick feet that proved beneficial at his old position with an ability to break tackles that goes beyond his size. Only eight of his 20 carries went for single-digit yards, and Marcoccio didn't take a loss on any of them.

"I've always been told I run angry," Marcoccio said. "I run a little bit different from other people. From our past running backs I've learned how to run hard, hit the hole, be fast and physical.

"I guess it's just a style I've built up."

Burrillville (4-0, Division II) used 20 unanswered points to take command after an opening touchdown pass by Quinones Diaz to Carlos Valentin, and the first came after a bit of a gamble. The Broncos dialed up a fake punt from their own 36 and Jack Belluzzi scampered 24 yards down the right side for a first down. Gavis hit Bannon five plays later from 4 yards out and added a 50-yard strike to the junior with just 13 seconds left in the first half.

"Everyone was saying, 'Fake punt, fake punt,'" Gavis said. "I was like, 'Why are we doing that on the first drive?' Coach Ferraro came up to me and said, 'We're not here to punt.'"

Belluzzi was quiet by his lofty standards – three catches on six targets for 36 yards. The Villa Novans (3-1) shadowed him with Quinones Diaz in man-to-man coverage and a safety over the top to help. Gavis still closed 8-for-13 passing and Burrillville moved on to another headliner next week against East Providence (4-0) in impressive style.

"We're going to have to get ready," Marcoccio said. "They're a great team. We're going to have to play harder than tonight – better than we did tonight."

title: Diatta signing positive but midfielder still required
description: BBC Radio 3CR's Geoff Doyle looks at Watford's latest signing and where the Hornets might turn their attention next.
fullText:
The signing of Krepin Diatta looks another shrewd piece of business by Watford.

This is a seasoned Champions League player who featured in every match at the World Cup with Senegal.

With his national team in the summer he was used at right-back but he has played higher up the pitch and as a winger. Watford have had full-back injury problems this season so this could be his initial position with the option of using him elsewhere as the season progresses.

Diatta was linked to Premier League clubs in the summer so it is interesting that he has joined the Hornets now and why he has been a free agent since early summer.

Nevertheless, if he is at the level he has been playing at for the past six years, it is a great addition for Watford.

We will now see whether the Hornets can sign a midfielder in this international break. It goes without saying the club will be looking, as this is the current problem area.

The signing of Diatta indicates what market Watford will be searching; it is unlikely to be a British player. The Hornets don't pay huge signing on fees and big wages to what they would consider journeymen English players.

That's not to say they don't need this type of player. In recent years many head coaches have bemoaned the lack of British players with Championship or English Football League experience.

But this has never been the transfer model at Vicarage Road nor is it ever likely to be under owner Gino Pozzo. Which is why it was so odd that chief executive Scott Duxbury and sporting director Luke Dowling said in the summer those type of players were targets in the transfer window.

Why say it? Young overseas bargains with a view to sell on has always been the Watford way under Pozzo.

Like so many other clubs, Watford have many players on international duty and will be desperately hoping none of them come back injured.

The casualty list is still high in the treatment room at London Colney with key midfielder Edoardo Bove not expected back until the next international break in November.

With Diatta and other late August signings, Watford potentially have a very strong starting 11 (when all fit). Whether the backup behind is good enough is another matter.

title: Texas QB Arch Manning’s uncle shares telling family standard ahead of draft decision
description: Eli Manning took the Arch Manning question on The Colin Cowherd Podcast, in an episode released on Thursday, Oct. 1, with his nephew four games into his second season as Texas’ starting quarterback. Eli skipped the timeline and described what the Mannings have always expected to get out of college, a standard the family’s own […] The post Texas QB Arch Manning’s uncle shares telling family standard ahead of draft decision appeared first on Gridiron Heroics.
fullText:
Eli Manning took the Arch Manning question on The Colin Cowherd Podcast, in an episode released on Thursday, Oct. 1, with his nephew four games into his second season as Texas' starting quarterback. Eli skipped the timeline and described what the Mannings have always expected to get out of college, a standard the family's own history has already tested.

Arch redshirted as a freshman in 2023, so he is a redshirt junior this fall with the 2027 season still available. He can declare for the 2027 NFL Draft after this season or play one more year in Austin and enter the 2028 draft.

Peyton Manning faced a version of that choice after the 1996 season, when he was widely viewed as the likely No. 1 pick, and went back to Tennessee anyway. "I didn't want to be 50 years old wondering what my senior year in college would have been like," Peyton said. That December, he threw for 373 yards and four touchdowns as the Vols came back to beat Auburn 30-29 in the SEC Championship Game, and he went first overall in 1998.

Eli redshirted at Ole Miss and still started four seasons before going first overall in 2004. Archie Manning played out his eligibility at Ole Miss before going second overall in 1971. In 2025, Archie said Arch would not enter the 2026 draft, which held up when Arch returned for this season. Asked about Arch now, Eli described the same approach.

"Yeah, that's the whole point of college, to enjoy being in college, to get better every year. It's opportunities to play more games, to get better, to get more prepared for the NFL. To try to win a national championship or an SEC championship, to be a captain of the team. Like, all those things were important to us," Eli said on The Colin Cowherd Podcast.

"It's not just about, hey, this is all about getting through the NFL and going to the next step. No, it's about enjoying your experience, enjoying your teammates, becoming a better player, becoming a better leader, building something special with the guys that have all been there together. So I'm proud of Arch and how he's handled this and his mindset," Eli added.

Former New York Giants QB Eli Manning seemingly confirmed that his nephew and Texas Longhorns QB Arch Manning is at least considering returning to college for one more season and declaring for the NFL Draft in 2028.

Arch is currently going through his second season as the… pic.twitter.com/IvhvC0M6Vb

— NFL Rumors (@nflrums) October 3, 2026

Arch's first full season as the starter in 2025 produced a 9-3 regular season and a 41-27 bowl win over Michigan, but no SEC title. No Manning has won a national championship, and Peyton remains the only one with an SEC crown. Texas was 4-0 after its Sept. 26 win at Tennessee, so the chase Eli described is open right now.

Arch reportedly made $6.5 million in NIL money in 2024. His uncles played college football long before players could collect anything like it, so another year at Texas costs Arch far less than it would have cost them.

Eli never said which draft Arch will enter, and Arch has not announced anything. The decision waits on a season that is barely a month old.

title: Who is Rui Pinto? The whistleblower abandoned by Portuguese authorities over Man City leaks
description: Pinto, the hacker who first revealed Man City’s financial cheating, has discovered he will lose his witness protection
fullText:
Manchester City find themselves at the centre of the biggest story in Premier League history as they face potential relegation or expulsion from a division they currently lead, after being found guilty of nearly all of the 115 charges levied against them.

But this scandal had humble beginnings.

Rui Pinto is the Portuguese hacker who blew the whistle on City's financial cheating, prompting an entire Premier League investigation.

Through his website Football Leaks, he published confidential documents that showed City broke league rules over a nine-season period in 2018. German newspaper Der Spiegel's subsequent investigative report detailing allegations against City was based on these documents.

Pinto was in other legal trouble by the time the City allegations took the football world by storm. After being unmasked as the man behind Football Leaks, he faced 147 charges that included computer fraud, attempted extortion and violating privacy of correspondence in Portugal, having published a number of stories about other players and clubs including those relating to Porto and Benfica. He was extradited from Hungary, where he had been living, in March 2019.

He described himself as a "whistleblower" and denied wrongdoing, claiming he was trying to expose "what was wrong with football". He spent more than a year in custody before going under house arrest before a criminal trial in Lisbon. In September 2023, he received a four-year suspended jail sentence and has been living under police witness protection at an undisclosed location since.

Upon learning the emphatic verdict in the City case, Pinto said: "The statement released today by the Premier League ultimately confirms, unequivocally, the truth of everything that was revealed through Football Leaks." It marks a victory eight years in the making for the 37-year-old.

However, the news has been followed by a hammer blow for Pinto. Less than 24 hours after the independent commission made City's guilt official, Pinto discovered he would lose his witness protection on Saturday 10 October. He will be forced out of his confidential residence and must find new housing; something which has been described "an act of state terrorism".

"His situation is now critical," said a joint statement from his Portuguese and French legal team. "The threats against him are not merely theoretical; he was assaulted in Lisbon last April.

"His revelations implicated powerful figures with vast resources, and many resulting legal proceedings are still ongoing, as evidenced by the decision handed down just days ago by the Premier League's independent commission regarding Manchester City.

"Abruptly deprived of his protected housing and plunged into a state of extreme precariousness, Rui Pinto would be more vulnerable now than at any time since 2020."

He has set up a GoFundMe requesting €3m after the Portuguese state "knowingly decided to put my life at risk".

"I have no alternative but to relocate, within the next few days, to an undisclosed location for an indefinite period of time, due to the multiple death threats I have received and the serious risk of an assassination attempt against me," he said.

title: Notre Dame Nabs Six Spots on Early NFL Draft Board
description: For decades, major football programs such as the Notre Dame Fighting Irish have spent heavily on training centers and experienced coaching staffs. Those resources help high school recruits become stronger and more prepared early in their college careers. Top universities now run football programs that work much like professional teams. Scouts follow talented college players […] The post Notre Dame Nabs Six Spots on Early NFL Draft Board appeared first on Gridiron Heroics.
fullText:
For decades, major football programs such as the Notre Dame Fighting Irish have spent heavily on training centers and experienced coaching staffs. Those resources help high school recruits become stronger and more prepared early in their college careers.

Top universities now run football programs that work much like professional teams. Scouts follow talented college players for years, while fans pay close attention to young players with strong physical skills.

On Thursday, sports media ESPN published its early player rankings for the 2027 professional football draft. Industry analyst Jordan Reid evaluated college athletes across the nation and selected six Notre Dame players for his top 50 list.

Leading this collegiate group, junior cornerback Leonard Moore earned the second overall spot. Reid wrote, "With excellent length, speed and technique, Moore is the prototypical cornerback prospect."

Because Moore allowed zero completed passes through late September, scouts consider him an elite defender. Furthermore, his teammate CJ Carr ranked 22nd on the national list after throwing for 963 yards and nine touchdowns.

Reid praised the young quarterback in his report, stating that Carr is a "refined pocket passer whose eyes, feet and throwing motion are always in cohesion." Consequently, Carr's accurate passing numbers elevated his status among professional evaluators.

Four additional Notre Dame athletes rounded out the prestigious board. Specifically, safety Brauntae Johnson earned the 26th position.

Subsequently, edge rusher Boubacar Traore secured spot 47 after producing 2.5 sacks this autumn. Linebacker Kyngstonn Viliamu-Asa was selected 48th.

Finally, offensive lineman Anthonie Knapp grabbed the 49th rank because he surrendered only a 0.9 percent pressure rate on 230 snaps.

NFL rules require players to be at least three years removed from high school before entering the draft. True juniors and redshirt sophomores may qualify, but true freshmen and true sophomores cannot declare before completing that waiting period.

The rule prevents true college sophomores from signing NFL contracts before the 2027 draft. An early ESPN ranking gives a player attention, but it does not offer a contract or guarantee any money.

NFL teams make their own decisions during the scouting process. They study game film, conduct medical checks and watch players complete athletic drills before making draft selections.

Strong media rankings can still bring national attention to a college program. However, NFL scouts follow their own watchlists and attend practices and games based on each team's evaluation plans.

Six Notre Dame players included in early media rankings are still college students. They remain active members of the team during the current season.

title: Dave Portnoy names the culprit behind his Big Noon Kickoff exit
description: Fox’s Big Noon Kickoff goes on the air Saturday from Minneapolis, ahead of Michigan’s noon ET game at Minnesota, without Dave Portnoy or the Barstool Sports personalities who joined the pregame show a little over a year ago. The Athletic reported on Friday that Barstool is off the Saturday broadcast. Portnoy confirmed it on X […] The post Dave Portnoy names the culprit behind his Big Noon Kickoff exit appeared first on Gridiron Heroics.
fullText:
Fox's Big Noon Kickoff goes on the air Saturday from Minneapolis, ahead of Michigan's noon ET game at Minnesota, without Dave Portnoy or the Barstool Sports personalities who joined the pregame show a little over a year ago. The Athletic reported on Friday that Barstool is off the Saturday broadcast. Portnoy confirmed it on X before he had even seen the story, and he came with his own explanation for it.

Portnoy wrote that Andrew Marchand never called him for a quote, then put the blame squarely on Columbus.

"Ohio State and Ryan Day b*tched and moaned to the Big 10 and threatened Fox till they had no choice. Juice wasn't worth the squeeze and frankly I don't blame them. Huge dollars at stake and you have Cryin Ryan throwing temper tantrums and making threats every few days on something I said. I always knew Ryan Day was soft but holy s**t even I didn't realize he was this soft," Portnoy wrote on X Friday night.

Just was told @AndrewMarchand is about to release an article saying I’ve been put on ice for @BNKonFOX I havent seen the article yet and he didnt call me for a quote but i can sum it up this way

Ohio State and Ryan Day bitched and moaned to the Big 10 and threatened Fox…

— Dave Portnoy (@stoolpresidente) October 3, 2026

I do not blame Ryan Day for me getting fired from WEEI, ESPN, or banned from the NFL

However he very certainly got me fired from @BNKonFOX #notorious https://t.co/beNX9COmD3

— Dave Portnoy (@stoolpresidente) October 3, 2026

Class recognizes class clearly https://t.co/ZQ8nVfxwfe

— Dave Portnoy (@stoolpresidente) October 3, 2026

The first show without him happens to be built around his own school. Portnoy, a Michigan graduate, made his Big Noon Kickoff debut in Columbus in August 2025. He sang the Michigan fight song on his way to the stage and peeled off a sweatshirt to reveal a "still can't beat Michigan" shirt in front of the Ohio State crowd.

Sources briefed on the decision told The Athletic there was no smoking gun. They described the ongoing struggle of fitting Barstool's persona inside Fox's more traditional show as unsustainable, which is a broader problem than one coach's objections.

Ahead of that 2025 debut, Portnoy made a similar claim, saying Ohio State had banned him from Ohio Stadium. Athletic director Ross Bjork denied any ban. He said Fox had decided Portnoy would not sit on the main desk, and that anyone off the desk did not appear on the field. A Big Ten spokesperson added that the league understood from Fox that Portnoy would not appear on the show's main stage inside any conference stadium that year.

Twice now, the decision on the record has belonged to Fox while Portnoy's version has put it on Day. Neither Fox nor Ohio State has publicly backed his account of Friday's news.

Wake Up Barstool keeps its weekday slot on FS1, and Portnoy said his relationship with the network remains strong. He also said Barstool's own college football show will keep traveling, possibly straight into enemy territory.

"The Barstool College Football will continue on. Maybe we'll even see you in Columbus where contrary to popular belief most fans love the rivalry and aren't p*ssies like Cryin Ryan," Portnoy wrote.

NFL hands down Jed York decision that mirrors past owner punishment

Steelers HC Mike McCarthy explains what happened during Aaron Rodgers hot mic moment

Browns' Jerry Jeudy sends honest message as Todd Monken makes role clear

title: Davide Ancelotti makes feelings clear on Vinicius Junior amid Real Madrid struggles
description: Real Madrid already had one of the most fearsome attacking lines on paper during the last two seasons, boasting some of the very best attacking players in Europe, including the likes of Kylian Mbappe,...
fullText:
Real Madrid already had one of the most fearsome attacking lines on paper during the last two seasons, boasting some of the very best attacking players in Europe, including the likes of Kylian Mbappe, Vinicius Junior, and Jude Bellingham. The Merengues strengthened this forward line even further this season by adding another star, Yan Diomande.

However, the team's attack has still not performed up to its expected standards. Concerns remain about the ability of Vinicius and Mbappe to perform at their optimal levels when playing together, while the Brazilian's form in itself has also raised a lot of disaffection among the fans.

Still, there is no doubt that he remains one of the most decisive players in world football. This was certainly the view of the former Real Madrid assistant coach Davide Ancelotti, who recently appeared in an interview with Diario AS, and commented on several aspects related to the Merengue club.

Despite fans' patience running thin with him, the younger Ancelotti explained why Vinicius is loved by his teammates:

"What can I say about Vini… He scored in two Champions League finals with us. I can only be grateful to him. It is no coincidence that a player everyone in the dressing room likes is so popular. Because he is generous. He never misses a training session. He doesn't hide, he doesn't deceive you, he never spares himself an effort, he never tells you, 'This hurts, so I'm not training.' He is always there for the team. And the players know that, which is why he is so well-liked."

The Italian highlighted what makes the Brazilian such a special player:

"When he is playing well, he is very difficult to contain. You have to be aware that you have a player like him because he has an impact on the team's overall balance. He has an impact because he is a very direct, very vertical player. He has so much confidence in his ability that he always takes on his man… And you need a structure behind him that allows you to play with him. If you don't have that, the game starts to become chaotic. Because Vini always goes for it, and always goes for it…"

"You are not going to change Vini, but what you can change is the structure behind him. And when he is in a positive spell, Vini decides matches for you. He has done it many times for Madrid."

The current Lille manager was asked about the presence of both Mbappe and Vinicius on the same team, to which he replied:

"(Laughs) You have to make the most of having a very vertical team, knowing that this will give you a lot, while also being prepared for what it takes away from you. Look, I'm not talking about the current Madrid team; I'm not here to solve anyone's problems, I have enough of my own… But Madrid have always had those players who don't give you as much control. And the important thing is that you don't allow the team to become stretched. That has always been the challenge."

On the other hand, Davide also recognized that Vinicius made a mistake by publicly protesting against Xabi Alonso's decision to sub him out last season:

"First of all, I felt sorry for Xabi because I have a good relationship with him. It wasn't right. Vini is the first to know that he made a mistake because you have to show respect to the coach, the club, your teammates and the fans. But it is in the past now. I don't think Madrid failed to win important trophies because of that moment."

Furthermore, the Italian highlighted that this gesture was not anything out of the ordinary, and Real Madrid dressing room is full of highly professional players:

"If that were the case, there would be no need for a coach. That doesn't reflect reality. Madrid's players are extremely professional. We never had a bad reaction from anyone. Do they not want to come off the pitch? Fine, that's normal. Kroos did what Vini did a thousand times. Modric did it in his own language. Casemiro does it… But that doesn't mean the players are in charge. The coach is in charge in the Madrid dressing room."

Having worked with him at both Real Madrid and the Brazil national team, Davide Ancelotti is in a particularly good position to know how to get the best out of Vinicius Junior. These comments can prove useful for Jose Mourinho, especially as it remains one of his main challenges to unlock the Brazilian's true potential and make the Merengue attack perform at its best level.

title: Will Colts' WR Keenan Allen play in Week 4 v. Commanders?

fullText:

title: ‘Elon is my prophet’: how Musk’s Doge team took a wrecking ball to Washington
description:
When the new ‘department of government efficiency’ sent young techies to disrupt federal agencies, not everyone complied. Here’s what happened when one worker fought to protect immigrant data
In the early hours of Saturday 22 February 2025 the following email landed in the inboxes of the entire US federal workforce:
From: HR hr@opm.gov
 Continue reading...
fullText:
When the new ‘department of government efficiency’ sent young techies to disrupt federal agencies, not everyone complied. Here’s what happened when one worker fought to protect immigrant data

In the early hours of Saturday 22 February 2025 the following email landed in the inboxes of the entire US federal workforce:

Sent: Saturday, February 22, 2025

Subject: What did you do last week?

Please reply to this email with approx. 5 bullets of what you accomplished last week and cc your manager.

Please do not send any classified information, links, or attachments.

Deadline is this Monday at 11:59 p.m. EST.

When she noticed the email that Saturday night, Kathleen Walters already had far too much going on in her life. Number one was figuring out if the lump in her breast that her doctor had just detected was a tumour. Half of her known blood relatives had died of cancer, and she was now 52: the lump needed understanding.

Her work life was harder to dramatise with a list. For a start, the specifics of her job at any given moment, as she would have been the first to point out, couldn’t legally be described to others. She was the chief privacy officer at the Internal Revenue Service. She ran a staff of 650 people tasked with preventing any of the 100,000 IRS employees from losing or leaking or even so much as peeking at, unless they had the authority to peek, any of the 266m tax returns they were just then processing from the previous year. “One hundred thousand people is a big-sized town,” said Kathleen. “In any big-sized town, you have some crazy people. I could easily see someone writing, ‘This weekend I audited Beyoncé.’”

Whoever had sent this email asking her to list five things she’d done at work was now demanding that all these people inside the IRS share information that, in many cases, should never be shared. She thought it was nuts.

She responded quickly, and vaguely, with five things she had done the previous week, all the while feeling sure no one would ever read what she wrote. Her phone was already exploding with questions from her subordinates – a few of whom were saying that their replies were bouncing back with a “mailbox is full” notice. Now she had to sit and think about how to minimise the damage that might be caused by 100,000 IRS employees thinking that they’d lose their jobs if they didn’t supply some detailed answer about what they’d done during their work week. A meaningful percentage risked being tossed in jail if they described what they did in an email. It was a crime for an IRS employee even to acknowledge that some specific person had or had not filed a tax return. “People don’t understand what the IRS does,” said Kathleen.

The email came as a surprise, but then the IRS was suddenly full of surprises. Nine days earlier, on 13 February, a Thursday, the first Doge person turned up in the lobby, unannounced, and security called Traci DiMartini, who ran the IRS’s human capital department. There’s a kid down here who said he needs to get into the building, he said. The kid’s name was Gavin Kliger.

Traci called her counterpart at the Treasury department, as the IRS sits inside Treasury, and Treasury always cleared any new political appointees; Treasury had no record of anyone named Gavin Kliger. Traci then called Tim Curry at the Office of Personnel Management – but he had no idea what was going on. Finally, she called security and asked them to escort the young man to her office.

Gavin Kliger came with a chip on his shoulder, it seemed to Traci. He offered not even the faintest smile or the most glancing eye contact. Dressed in black from hoodie to sneaker, he was brusque to the point of rudeness. He looked, and was, just a few years out of college. Eyes on the floor, he explained to Traci that he’d come to sort out the problems inside the IRS and to root out the fraud. “That’s a big job!” she said.

Anyone who worked at the IRS knew that it had its problems; fraud wasn’t likely one of them. Its technology infrastructure was a case study in government dysfunction, but its ethical infrastructure was sound. Like all federal employees, its staff wasn’t allowed to accept more than a free cup of coffee from anyone who might want something from their agency.

Gavin Kliger, in contrast, struck Traci as problematic. He’d somehow laid his hands on badges granting him access to some crazy number of government buildings. His backpack was stuffed with government-issue phones and at least four laptops – and he was now insisting that Traci supply him with an IRS phone and laptop. He also demanded his own IRS email address, access to computer systems with all the taxpayer information, and a meeting with the acting IRS commissioner, Doug O’Donnell. As Gavin sat there, Traci called Treasury again. That guy you said didn’t exist is now here sitting in my office. What do y’all want me to do with him?

The Treasury guy went away, then came back and said that Gavin Kliger had been hired three weeks earlier by the Office of Personnel Management and was attached to Doge – whatever that meant.

In her nine years running human capital departments at various federal agencies, Traci had never seen a new political appointee just turn up in the lobby and demand access to the computer systems. “None of this is normal,” she said, “but we’re still trying to be nice.” She explained to Gavin the IRS rules: before anyone was allowed to work inside the building, he needed to pass a tax audit.

I don’t need to do that, he said.

They went back and forth like that a bit until finally Gavin relented. Traci then explained that after he passed the audit, he’d need to be given the mandatory presentations about ethics and taxpayer information. Gavin thought that the IRS should just let him in. “He wanted access to our systems immediately,” said Traci.

Traci’s next call, at 6.30pm that Thursday evening, was to Kathleen, to arrange for her to brief Gavin on data privacy laws and to warn her that the experience might not be entirely pleasant. If I had a kid who behaved the way he does, I’d slap the shit out of him, Traci said – but then Traci was from Philadelphia. Traci was always telling Kathleen that she should try a bit less hard to see the best in others.

Phyllis, who loved working for Kathleen and saw falling on hand grenades as part of her job, never told her how this one had felt. She knew Gavin had expressed enthusiasm for white nationalists, and he likely knew that she knew. She tried to break the ice by walking in with her hand extended; Gavin stared at it and declined to shake it, though he had shaken the hands of the white men who had offered them. “He was kind of cool towards me,” said Phyllis. Before she could even start the briefing, he said, You know, I’ve heard these rules before at other agencies. Yes, she said, but these rules are different, because no other agency is governed by this privacy law, and this law can get you thrown in jail very quickly. As she walked him through the basics – how you can’t use your personal phone for business, how if you happen to so much as glimpse a form 1040 with someone’s name on it you must avert your eyes – Gavin played on his phone. “He’s multitasking right in front of me, typing and texting,” said Phyllis. “It was, here’s a routine that I must endure.”

It fell to Kathleen to draft the five-page agreement required by law for Gavin Kliger to be let inside the IRS building on Monday morning, 17 February. The memo that she wrote over the weekend, and that he signed, gave him access to some of the systems but, explicitly, none that contained taxpayer information.

Traci set him up in a conference room with an assistant at the beginning of the week. “People started getting these calls,” said Kathleen. “It was like getting the call from the principal’s office. ‘Gavin wants to see you.’ ”

Doge had its own private structure in addition to its official one. Officially, President Trump created Doge with an executive order on his first day in office. The president doesn’t have the authority to create or to fund an executive agency, however. Congress does. The Trump administration dodged that problem by taking an office inside the White House created during the second Obama term, the US Digital Service, kicking out the people inside and renaming it the Department of Government Efficiency. The US Digital Service had been given the power to hire talent from the tech sector without going through the usual slow federal hiring process. This now ensured that Doge could hire whomever it wanted without any questions being asked, and make it sound official. In effect, all that Doge had done was create a corpse for itself to occupy.

The zombie killed off the spirit of the original life form.  Real Doge had nothing to do with Official Doge or the former US Digital Service or any other government body. Real Doge was more like Elon Musk’s pop-up restaurant. “None of us ever signed a piece of paper saying that we were in Doge,” said one Doge insider. The people who joined either worked for one of Musk’s companies, or knew someone who did, or knew someone who knew someone who did. To be truly a member of Doge was to be included in the group Signal chat and granted access to the sleeping quarters on the sixth floor of the General Services Administration (GSA).

Official Doge employed maybe 10 guys in their 40s and 50s who wore suits and could sort of pass as ordinary political appointees, but none had access to the sixth floor at GSA. “The older guys in the suits were not there to take risks or blow things up,” said one Doge insider. It was hard to say what any of the older Doge suits did except to make way for the young guys when they showed up with explosives.

Most of Doge’s inner circle just wanted to exist in the presence of Elon Musk. “It was, Elon is my prophet, and I worship the ground he walks on,” said one of the older Doge insiders.

As a Doge member, you could get away with saying – or having said – almost anything. What you couldn’t say is that the government actually sort of worked. Or, if it didn’t work, why it didn’t work. This new game rewarded not understanding but speed. The plan was the same plan Musk had executed two years earlier at Twitter: Make sweeping statements about the incompetence and dishonesty of the people working inside the place before you know much about them. Once you’ve terrified the employees, fire them in huge numbers. If it turns out you screwed up and fired the wrong people, hire some of them back.

The people who rallied to the cause and felt qualified to execute Elon Musk’s vision for the federal government shared certain qualities. They were mostly young white males. They were mostly from upper-middle-class or rich families. Most knew or pretended to know how to program a computer. Not all of them, but enough of them for there to be a pattern, had been rejected from the most selective colleges and universities and ended up feeling they’d been screwed by the admissions process. They landed at Penn instead of Princeton, or the University of Nebraska instead of Harvard, with a grievance that added to the foundation of their politics. They thought of themselves as the smartest people in the room and couldn’t understand why the rest of the room didn’t simply stand up and cheer. In Washington they borrowed from Elon Musk their status and sense of superiority. They also seemed to share his pleasure in the idea of people being afraid of them.

Even among the young men sleeping inside the GSA, Gavin was regarded as a force. “Wherever he went, entropy went through the roof,” said one. Just weeks into their new jobs as destroyers of government institutions, the Muskrats had given Gavin Kliger a nickname: the Chaos Agent.

Another surprising email landed in Kathleen’s inbox on 28 February. It was Friday night. “I don’t know why everything always happened on a Friday night,” she said. She’d taken her daughter for pizza and wasn’t meant to be checking her phone when she spotted the emails. The first one that she read had been sent at 6.34pm by a colleague in the IRS legal department. “Melanie requested a data pull,” it read. “It feels not quite kosher.”

Exactly 64 minutes earlier, at 5.30pm, Doug O’Donnell, the acting IRS commissioner, had left his post. O’Donnell’s successor was to be Melanie Krause, until then chief operating officer, who had been installed as acting IRS commissioner by Treasury secretary Scott Bessent. Like Kathleen, Melanie was a career civil servant, though 13 years younger. Kathleen had considered her a friend. “She was really smart, and I thought she meant well,” said Kathleen. “She wasn’t a mean person.” They were both working moms, and Melanie liked to share, and share in, the details of the difficulties. Now she’d apparently told the IRS research department to share taxpayer data. With whom, and for what purpose, became clear in the second email, which came from the IRS director of data management:

DHS [the Department of Homeland Security] has requested if we could find addresses for 700,000 names of likely undocumented immigrants.

1. Do we have legal authority to use the tax return filing data for this purpose?

2. If the answer to Question 1 is yes, then my second question is related to a file we receive from the Social Security Administration (SSA) that contains Date of Birth (DOB), Date of Death (DOD), Gender, Citizenship, and Name Control Information for all issued Social Security Numbers (SSN). Would our MOU allow us to use this perhaps in conjunction to tax return data for this purpose?

While it is likely that use of SSA data is also needed. The technical feasibility of being able to produce reliable outcome is unknown but likely very low.

Kathleen read the first numbered paragraph and stopped reading. The request was plainly illegal. The IRS couldn’t just hand over great gobs of taxpayer information to the Department of Homeland Security or any other agency without a change in federal privacy law. Changing the law was not trivial. She knew that because she’d just done it – to allow the IRS to share taxpayer data with state child support enforcement agencies. The states wanted to know if former spouses who were failing to pay child support in fact did not have the income to do so – and the IRS alone could answer the question. What Kathleen had asked for in that case could not have been less controversial. Basically no one in American politics was willing to come out against child support enforcement, and the change to the federal law had passed Congress in December 2024 with almost no dissent. Yet it had taken 18 months to get it done, with endless meetings on Capitol Hill and the close involvement of the IRS commissioner and the secretary of health and human services. “Doge couldn’t imagine 18 months,” she said. “Doge didn’t have 18 months. Their whole thing was, If you can’t do it legally, we’ll find some way to do it illegally.”

This, Kathleen realised, is how they could grab taxpayer data illegally. By doing it on a Friday night. Using a woman, Melanie Krause, about to take over as acting commissioner, after a 10-minute meeting between her and Scott Bessent. Without informing the executive charged with protecting the information. “She went around me because she knew what my answer is,” said Kathleen.

The violation ran deeper than the law. The specific dataset sought by DHS was in a silo reserved for the tax returns filed by people without social security numbers. The IRS had created the so-called Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (Itin) back in 1996 as a mechanism for undocumented workers and other non-citizens who lacked social security numbers to file a return and pay taxes.

The programme had been a huge success. The IRS had collected hundreds of billions of dollars in taxes through it. Undocumented workers had been able to demonstrate their commitment to the country, and ease their path to citizenship, by paying more than their fair share. (They were still excluded from most federal benefits.) Now DHS wanted their private data, and it wasn’t hard for Kathleen or anyone else at the IRS to see why. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (Ice) had gone hunting undocumented workers but lacked reliable home addresses for many of them. The tax returns told you where roughly 7 million of them might be found.

The second Trump administration had a gift for creating such moments. It was as if all at once all these characters in a grand masked ball were forced to remove their disguises and reveal their identities. In the Great Unmasking, the nation’s leading law firms, led by Paul, Weiss, would cave to what amounted to Trump’s blackmail demands to avoid being shut out of federal business. The nation’s research universities, led by Columbia, would change their internal policies and even pay fines to avoid losing federal dollars.

The revealing moments in the civil service were lonelier. They occurred inside people’s hearts and minds, and seldom leaked to the press. After his arrival at the IRS, one of Gavin Kliger’s first acts had been to demand that the agency fire its 6,700 probationary workers, who had yet to be granted civil service protection. By law they could be fired only for poor performance. Gavin had asked Traci DiMartini, in her capacity as head of human resources, to agree to put her name on an email to the mostly young employees telling them that they had failed at their jobs. The Doge people played this trick often. They’d use or try to use civil servants as a kind of ventriloquist dummy so that they, the Doge workers, could keep their names off official documents. But Traci took one look at the email, saw it was plainly a lie, and refused to have anything to do with it. The price of that single act of resistance was her job. Gavin didn’t have the authority to fire Traci, but his new acting commissioner did. “He asked Melanie to fire Traci, and Melanie did it,” said Kathleen.

Melanie Krause’s predecessor, Doug O’Donnell, had been pushed out by Doge after he, too, refused to send the dishonest email to the IRS’s 6,700 probationary workers. When a Doge guy at Treasury called with the order, O’Donnell, who had worked for the agency for 38 years, said he wanted to sleep on it – then had trouble sleeping. “He was struggling with this notion of sending the termination emails with this false justification for the termination,” said a person in whom O’Donnell confided. The next day, he refused to send the email, and the Doge guy said something like, “Well, let me be the first to congratulate you on your retirement.” Melanie had been installed precisely because she was proving to Doge that she was more pliable.

Standing outside the pizza place with her daughter in late February, Kathleen called Melanie. Ever since Melanie had arrived, in the fall of 2021, she had sought Kathleen’s advice. There had been stretches when they met daily. Kathleen just sort of assumed that, faced with a difficult choice, Melanie would do what Kathleen herself would do. “I don’t really get outraged,” said Kathleen. “But I think people need to be confronted when they have done something inappropriate.”

Melanie, what are you doing? she asked. We already have legal opinions about this, and it is obviously against the law.

I didn’t tell them to do it, said Melanie. I told them to think about how to do it – if it was legal.

But she hadn’t asked anyone to find out if it was legal to send Ice the home addresses of 700,000 undocumented workers – culled, somehow, from the 7 million who had paid taxes. She’d told them to send the data over, on a Friday night. In such a way that Kathleen might never have heard about it – or heard too late.

It’s not going to be any more legal on Saturday, said Kathleen.

Let’s meet on Monday to clear things up, said Melanie.

They didn’t meet. Instead, on Monday – 3 March – Kathleen and several other top IRS leaders were called into a meeting with Gavin Kliger.

I’ve figured out something important about the IRS, Gavin said. He paused for effect.

Every agency has a superpower, said Gavin. The IRS’s superpower is data.

Everyone in the agency knew that its data was valuable. That was the reason for the strict laws that prevented it from being exploited for profit or political gain. “He said this in a way that he expected everyone to clap when he was done,” said Kathleen.

“No one said a word.” The people around the table – a group that included a woman who had worked at the IRS for 54 years, or 53 years and 50 weeks longer than Gavin Kliger – looked down, or away. Kathleen felt embarrassed for Gavin Kliger. But now it was clear what the meeting was about. Gavin wanted, in his words, “to explore how we can share our data with other agencies”.

Interestingly, he never once mentioned Ice or DHS. Instead, that week, he sought to share data with himself, by trying to access files detailing IRS contracts with outside consultants that also contained taxpayer information. Kathleen denied him access.

The following Monday, she received a cryptic text from a senior IRS official. I’m going to call your cell, but don’t answer, it read. Her phone rang and she dutifully stared at it. Then came the second text: Gavin is asking where your office is and is now trying to find you to fire you because he says you’re the blocker.

The Blocker! It was one of Elon’s favourite terms. The blocker was the person who didn’t understand progress. The person without vision. The person who could not see beyond the way things were to the way they ought to be. The person who didn’t want to live on Mars or possibly even care if anyone ever got there. The inferior person. Traci had been a blocker. Find the blockers between us and what we want, Elon told his young followers. Find the blockers and eliminate them. Maybe more than anything else, Doge wanted the data. Kathleen was the person blocking them from getting it.

She wasn’t sure what she’d done to anger Gavin. It could have been limiting his access to the procurement contracts. It could also have been pushing back on his request to grant Palantir, Doge’s favourite federal contractor, the right to work with taxpayer data. What Gavin’s issue likely was not was her resistance to handing over to the Department of Homeland Security the addresses of taxpayers who lacked social security numbers. Gavin had never brought that up; this particular attempt to break the law wasn’t his idea. It was coming from somewhere else. As she thought she had stopped it, she ceased to worry about it.

And so, roughly two weeks later, on Thursday, 27 March, she was caught completely off guard by an email chain that popped up on her screen. At the bottom was its origin: a note from Melanie, forwarding some document from the IRS legal department, along with what sounded like an innocuous request. “Kathleen, could you help facilitate I won’t be able to join today?” it read, without explaining what she was meant to facilitate or why Melanie wouldn’t be able to join. Scrolling through, Kathleen couldn’t find the document but did see lots of bewildered replies from others who had been included – What is this about? Happy to help but can you tell us what this is? She called the two young lawyers in the IRS legal office who had authored the document referred to in the chain that had somehow gone missing. They explained that the thing Melanie wanted Kathleen to facilitate was a memorandum of understanding for the IRS to share taxpayer data with DHS. Kathleen was knocked sideways. “I thought that it had been stopped,” she said. “I thought Melanie had been caught with her pants down.” The young lawyers now told her that not only had it not been stopped: they’d been working on it since the end of February. “They told me that they were sorry but Melanie had told them to do it and not to tell me or their boss,” said Kathleen.

The situation was obviously bizarre. Kathleen had never heard of an IRS director asking young IRS lawyers to work on something on the side without telling their boss. And if Melanie didn’t want Kathleen to know that she was handing IRS data to DHS, why had she suddenly included her in the conversation? “I think she got scared and dumped it on me to sign off on,” said Kathleen. Melanie was doing to Kathleen what Gavin Kliger had done to Traci DiMartini. She was presenting her with her own unmasking moment and forcing her to make a choice.

Instead of signing off, Kathleen arranged a Zoom call that day, with the people at the Department of Homeland Security who were requesting the data. The “ICE Innovation Lab”, they called themselves. She’d never heard of it. When she Googled it, nothing came up.

A few others joined the call – lawyers from DHS and a privacy lawyer at the IRS named Julie Schwartz. On the call, Kathleen explained that there were some very narrow circumstances that would allow the IRS to lend a hand. If, for example, an undocumented worker had murdered someone and the police had issued a warrant for his arrest. The Ice Innovators explained that they were looking for more than wanted criminals. “Just how many people do you want information on?” asked Kathleen. The Ice Innovators went back and forth between themselves before agreeing that the number was 7 million. They wanted the current addresses of 7 million undocumented workers who had paid their taxes. The most law-abiding, it turned out, might be the easiest to catch.

After the call, Julie, the IRS privacy lawyer, came straight to her office. Julie was usually ice-calm – someone who kept her wits about her. She hadn’t a trace of drama in her. But now Julie was not calm. Kathleen, after that call I’m not working on this thing, she said. I’m not coming in tomorrow. I might not come in Monday. I might not come in ever again.

“I don’t usually deal with life or death stuff,” said Kathleen. “But this was life or death stuff. At that moment I knew I had to quit. Either that or I’m going to get fired, because I can’t facilitate something that will break the law and is going to hurt people. We all have boundaries. That was my boundary.”

That weekend, Kathleen sent Melanie a note saying she’d be resigning. “I didn’t need to tell her why,” said Kathleen. “She knew why.” She’d be leaving just weeks before her 20th anniversary with the agency. If she’d waited until mid-May, she would have been able to retire and receive benefits for the rest of her life. But she didn’t want to retire. Federal law made it hard for a retired civil servant to return, and if the day ever came when the IRS was rebuilt, she wanted to be able to return. She’d just learned that the lump in her breast was benign.

Days later, Melanie beat Kathleen to it and resigned. Kathleen never figured out how much her note to Melanie – and with it the increased likelihood that the attempted data heist would wind up in the press – led Melanie to quit. On her way out the door, Melanie asked the IRS’s head of communications to plant a story in the Washington Post that she was leaving as a matter of principle. The story cast Melanie as a martyr who had quit rather than divulge IRS data to DHS, when Kathleen knew that she had been caught red-handed trying to do precisely that. “I completely misjudged her character,” said Kathleen.

The Ice agents came for the “illegals” long after the property managers had gone home. The only evidence left behind were grainy videos on security cameras and accounts of terrified residents. “They’re coming in the nights, unannounced,” said Antonio Marquez, who ran a company that owned and managed apartment buildings scattered across the south and south-western United States occupied mostly by lower-middle-income Latinos. “We don’t know how they are targeting the units. It’s wreaking complete havoc.”

Antonio’s apartment complex outside Austin houses a thousand people, mostly young families, at least half of whom are undocumented. It had been visited in the spring late at night by teams of Ice agents. They came in unmarked cars, reported the tenants who remained after the raid. They had no warrants and read no rights. They knew, or thought they knew, exactly which doors to jimmy and which locks to pick and which people to take. The next morning a bunch of tenants were simply gone. All that remained was a pile of discarded possessions.

After the first Austin raid, Antonio had erected a tall metal fence around the property. Occasionally, the Ice agents had taken fully documented tenants – including an older woman who always paid on time, and who returned from Ice custody in an ankle bracelet. The great mystery to Antonio was how Ice knew where people lived. “These are fully targeted,” he said. “They already had these people in mind. They have their addresses. And we don’t know how they’re getting them.”

He was too busy doing his job to notice when, on 11 February 2026, the Washington Post reported that the IRS had shared with the Department of Homeland Security the tax data of 47,000 undocumented workers. On the heels of the Post’s scoop, a federal judge hearing a case on the subject summoned the IRS lawyers who had previously sworn that the agency had rebuffed the DHS demands. Under questioning, the lawyers confessed that the agency had lied to the court and that it had in fact shared the data. “The IRS violated the [Internal Revenue Code] approximately 42,695 times by disclosing last known taxpayer addresses to Ice,” the judge wrote in her opinion.

On a hot, sunny afternoon in early March in north-east Austin, it is a lot quieter than it was a year ago, back when Kathleen Walters was still a blocker. Two small children play in a pool, and a worn middle-aged man squats warily in a corner, smoking a cigarette. The wall of the office where the remaining residents come for their mail is decorated with posters advertising the services that Antonio’s company offers. One is more official-looking than the others. Free File del IRS, it reads across the top – and just below, in finer print, it explains how easy and painless it is for a non-citizen to file their taxes.

This is an edited extract from Blockers: Rebels in the Deep State by Michael Lewis, published by Allen Lane (£25). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

title: OpenAI says its review into hacks, including on Australian government sites, is costing $500,000 a day
description: Company says it is reviewing 50 petabytes of data after its agents accessed websites including Medicare without...
fullText:
Company says it is reviewing 50 petabytes of data after its agents accessed websites including Medicare without authorisation

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

OpenAI says its review in response to the Medicare and Hugging Face agent attacks is costing the company more than US$500,000 per day, as it deploys AI to examine data that would take a human 66m years to read.

The company has warned the review is ongoing, and more organisations may be informed they’ve been targeted in the near future.

On Friday evening, OpenAI revealed agents had hacked into a New South Wales government website in June and accessed historical non-public data on bushfires without authorisation.

It is the sixth government website in Australia to be notified by the AI giant since last month of agent activity on their services, after the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, announced OpenAI’s agents had hacked into Services Australia’s Medicare statistics portal.

The reason for the delay compared to the revelation of the Medicare attack is due to the sheer volume of data OpenAI needs to review.

In a blog post this week the company revealed the large amount of work involved in reviewing its agents’ activity.

OpenAI said it has to review 50 petabytes of data – roughly 50m gigabytes.

“We’re working back through the records month by month, looking for potential unintended activity beyond the cases we’ve already found,” the company said.

“To put that in perspective, if that were all plain English text, it would take one person about 66 million years to read it at 240 words a minute, reading nonstop without ever sleeping or taking a break.”

The company is searching records for where models accessed and changed websites, or took actions involving passwords, application programming interface (API) access or other sensitive credentials.

AI is being used to help sift through the records, and it was costing the company more than half a million US dollars per day to go through. OpenAI said it also plans to increase its computing power as the process is refined.

As of late last month, more than 100 organisations had been notified of having being targeted by OpenAI’s agents, but the company said notifying an organisation does not mean private information was accessed or that their system was compromised.

OpenAI said it expects to find more cases and notify more organisations about events that may have occurred months ago.

Organisations will be informed privately if they need to investigate and address potential security issues, and OpenAI has said it will publicly report findings about agent behaviour and identified weaknesses in safeguards for the broader AI sector.

“We err on the side of notification when our models’ activity exposes a potential security vulnerability, even in cases where it is unclear if the information accessed was intended to be public, so the organization can investigate and take appropriate action,” OpenAI said.

OpenAI discovered the latest NSW government website breach on Tuesday, and informed the state government and the Australian Signals Directorate after a 48-hour review.

The Medicare breach has prompted the Australian government to require departments and agencies to undertake a stocktake of legacy technology to reduce the number of ageing systems within government and reduce the cybersecurity risk they may present in the event of an AI agent attack.

Executives from OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and Google will front a joint parliamentary committee on artificial intelligence in Sydney on Tuesday.
