title: Why beating Denmark matters to Wales' Euro 2028 hopes
description: Avoiding finishing bottom of their Nations League group is a major aim for Wales following a win over Erling Haaland's Norway.
fullText:
There has not been much time for Craig Bellamy and Wales to enjoy their Nations League win over Norway.

After taking one Scandinavian scalp, the task is to claim another as Denmark come to Cardiff City Stadium on Sunday (19:45 BST).

Victory would mean recording back-to-back wins over higher-ranked nations for the first time in more than a decade.

It also offers an opportunity to take a huge step towards securing their top-tier Nations League status – and significantly boost their Euro 2028 qualification hopes.

Live on BBC iPlayer, BBC Two Wales, BBC Sounds, BBC Radio Wales, Radio Cymru and 5 Live, BBC Sport website and app, plus live text commentary.

Was long-awaited win a turning point for Bellamy?

Bellamy responds to abuse as Norway win lifts mood

Wales beat 10-man Norway to end winless run

Wales' win over Norway was their first in this Nations League A campaign, and followed opening defeats in Portugal and Denmark.

This is Wales' second crack at League A, having suffered immediate relegation without a win in their previous campaign at this level under Rob Page in 2022.

Bellamy has stated the aim is to avoid a similar fate this time around.

Thursday's win over Norway did not move Wales from the bottom of Group A4, meaning they trail the Danes and Norway on goal difference.

Beating Denmark would keep Wales' fate in their own hands going into next month's final fixtures against Norway in Oslo on 14 November and Portugal in Cardiff three days later.

The good news is that Wales could still stay in League A even if they finish bottom.

Because of a tweak to the format for the next Nations League in 2028-29, fewer sides will be demoted at the conclusion of this edition.

Previously, the bottom teams from each of the four League A groups were automatically relegated, with the four sides that finished third going into a relegation/promotion play-off against the four runners-up from League B.

This time, however, only the two worst-performing bottom sides go down – with the remaining pair going into the two-legged play-offs in March 2027.

Furthermore, the two best-performing third-placed sides are assured of their status, with the next two heading into the play-offs.

Ranking is based on points, goal difference, and the usual tie-breaking criteria.

Currently, Wales are the best of the fourth-placed sides, and a win over Denmark would really give them hope of avoiding play-offs altogether.

Not only that, it would keep alive hopes of finishing second and the chance to enter next spring's Nations League knock-outs, with two-legged quarter-finals to take place in March.

It is not just about the pride – or the prize pot – of staying in League A.

Seeding for Euro 2028 qualifying is based on where teams finish in the Nations League's overall ranking.

Wales will co-host the Euros with England, Republic of Ireland and Scotland but will go through the standard qualifying process.

The draw takes place in Belfast on 6 December, with the teams split into 12 groups, with the he seeds decided by Nations League rankings.

That means the best-performing 12 sides after next month's final fixtures will be kept apart as first seeds.

In other words, if Wales can avoid finishing bottom, they will be a top seed for the draw and avoid facing any of the big guns.

All of the co-hosting nations will be kept apart in the draw and will attempt to qualify automatically, but two places will be reserved at the finals should any of those host nations fail to qualify.

title: Second Israel game won't be a friendly - Hallgrimsson
description: Republic of Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson admits Sunday's second game against Israel is "not going to be a friendly" following comments from the latter's camp after last week's match in Hungary.
fullText:
Republic of Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson admits Sunday's second game against Israel is "not going to be a friendly" following comments from the latter's camp after last week's match in Hungary.

Having faced calls to boycott the Nations League fixtures because of the ongoing Israel-Gaza war, the Republic of Ireland did not engage in pre-match formalities and bowed their heads during the Israeli national anthem in Debrecen.

After a 3-0 win for the Republic of Ireland, Israel captain Manor Solomon said "we have a country 10 times better than theirs".

"Obviously they hate us. We don't like them," he added.

Following Thursday's 2-2 draw with Austria in Dublin, Hallgrimsson was asked if those comments will make for a tense encounter with Israel in Sunday's behind-closed-doors game in the Serbian town of Backla Topola.

"I guess so it's not going to be a friendly," said Hallgrimsson.

Hallgrimsson has spoken about the toll the controversy surrounding the Israel fixtures has had on his squad and said fatigue because of "everything going on" was a factor on Thursday as Austria fought back following Troy Parrott's first-half double.

"It is going to be tricky and challenging for the players to be ready [for Israel], but we will do everything and the medical team will work day and night to get them fit and fresh for that game," he added.

"[It's] just another football match, but [there] is more at stake for all of us."

The Israel fixtures have dominated this international window with the Republic of Ireland urged to withdraw from the games by the 'Stop The Game' campaign - organised by the pressure group Irish Sport for Palestine - who staged protests outside the Aviva Stadium before the Austria game.

The first half of Thursday's game was also briefly interrupted by a tennis ball protest and a pitch invader.

Hallgrimsson said he had worried prior to the match about the atmosphere inside Aviva Stadium but said the squad were buoyed by the support they received.

"Yeah, I'm not going to lie. I didn't know what to expect," said the 59-year-old.

"Obviously, the 'Stop the Game' protest is loud. I don't know how many but it's been loud, but it was just good to see the support from the fans and I just want to repeat the appreciation for people showing up and showing support tonight, it helps us a lot.

"It gives us even more pride to play for the country."

Before last week's game in Debrecen, Republic of Ireland goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu made himself unavailable for both Israel matches, saying he felt "it would be wrong to participate".

On the eve of the Israel game, the Republic of Ireland players' vote on whether to play the game passed by what Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell called a "significant majority".

When asked if he feels the support during the Austria game will help the players heading into the second Israel fixture, Hallgrimsson said: "I don't know, you'll have to ask them.

"I hope so. I hope we all feel more appreciated than probably before this match. If that answers the question, I think we feel more appreciated."

Sunday's game is the Republic of Ireland's 'home' fixture, which was moved to TSC Arena in Backa Topola amid ongoing fan protests from fans over the FAI's decision to fulfil the fixtures.

Hallgrimsson added he knows "absolutely nothing" about the town, which is around 100 miles north of Belgrade, Serbia's capital.

"Everything about this [is strange]," he said.

"First of all, the four-game window has been strange and challenging and testing. It will be different playing in front of 45,000 or 50,000 supporters and then playing in an empty stadium.

"But that's just another angle of the story and we need to be ready for that one."

title: India beat Pakistan to take Asian Games gold
description: Abhishek Sharma and Tilak Varma set India on their way to victory as they beat Pakistan to win gold at the Asian Games.
fullText:
Asian Games final, Nagoya, Japan

India 211-6 (20 overs): Abhishek 61 (28), Tilak 51* (22)

Pakistan 192-6 (20 overs): Nawaz 96 (51); Axar 2-29

Blistering half-centuries from Abhishek Sharma and Tilak Varma set India on their way to victory as they beat fierce rivals Pakistan by 19 runs to win gold at the Asian Games.

Having opted to bat first in Nagoya, India racked up a commanding 211-6 with Abhishek smashing seven sixes as he made 61 from 28 balls at the top of the order.

A stunning start helped the defending champions reach 81-2 at the end of the powerplay as Abhishek dominated the bowling before falling in the eighth over.

But the runs kept coming and Tilak's unbeaten 51 from 22, which featured three fours and four sixes, kept the momentum going until the end of innings.

Pakistan were soon in trouble in the chase, slipping to 39-3 and, despite a superb knock of 96 from Hasan Nawaz, they came up well short.

Nawaz bludgeoned seven maximums in a defiant innings but was left playing a lone hand and fell to the last ball of the match as Pakistan finished on 192-6.

The wickets were shared among the India bowlers with spinners Axar Patel and Washington Sundar both taking 2-29, while all-rounder Shivam Dube took 2-33.

After coming out on top four years ago in Hangzhou, China in their debut in the men's competition, India have now secured back-to-back golds.

title: Learning from Arteta and inspiring youngsters - Wilshere on management
description: Luton Town manager Jack Wilshere speaks about being back where he started as an eight-year-old and the lessons he learned from his time at Arsenal.
fullText:
The Football Interview will be available on BBC One at 12:45 BST every Saturday during the Premier League season, as well as on BBC iPlayer, BBC Football YouTube and the BBC Sport website and app.

In the seventh episode of the new season, Kelly Somers sits down with Luton Town manager Jack Wilshere.

Jack Wilshere's footballing career has gone full circle.

From starting out at Luton Town aged seven, Wilshere went on to win trophies at Arsenal and represent England at two major tournaments, before having to retire early because of injury problems and moving into coaching.

Now, he is back where he began, at Luton, this time as manager.

Sitting overlooking the pitches he used to play on as a youngster, the 34-year-old spoke to BBC Sport's Kelly Somers for The Football Interview and discussed his career - and how he hopes he can use his experiences to improve his players.

An exciting attacking midfielder with an ability to spot a pass or dribble past his opponent, Wilshere twice won the FA Cup with the Gunners.

He played in the Premier League 182 times and represented England on 34 occasions, appearing at both the World Cup in Brazil in 2014 and the European Championship in France two years later.

But injuries plagued the latter part of his career, with him announcing his retirement at only 30.

However, there were no regrets.

"I loved it [my career], I'm really proud," he said in the interview, which can be watched on BBC One at 12:45 BST on Saturday, 3 October.

"I got to play for my country and represent them at two major tournaments. OK, they didn't go the way we wanted them to, but I got to do it.

"I scored for my country, I played for the club I loved growing up, so pride is the biggest thing."

Watch The Football Interview on BBC Sport

Jack Wilshere - The Football Interview

On 13 October it will be one year since Wilshere became Luton boss, his first senior management role - although he had been in interim charge of Norwich City for a two-game spell at the end of the previous season.

He has already won silverware in his time with the Hatters, guiding them to the EFL Trophy, beating Stockport County 3-1 at Wembley in April in front of a crowd of nearly 50,000.

"I'm 34 now and probably could still be playing," he added. "Don't get me wrong, I loved every minute of playing, but I also really, really love this and I'm fortunate to start my [management] journey early.

"I'm really grateful to the club and the board for giving me that opportunity because they didn't need to. I was a young coach wanting to make my first step into the game."

Immediately after his playing career ended, he was invited back to Arsenal to coach their youngsters and instantly knew management and coaching was for him.

"I hear stories about people struggling in retirement and I retired on a Monday, and I was in with the [under] 18s on a Tuesday," said Wilshere. "When I first went and walked through the door to coaching, I realised this is going to take over my life, and I need to commit myself to this if I want to improve."

Arteta guided the Gunners to the Premier League title in 2025-26, their first time as English champions in 22 years, and Wilshere felt the Spaniard had played a vital role in developing him as a coach.

"I got to see Mikel and how he coached and the influence he was having," said Wilshere. "I would ask him questions, why he's doing certain things, and I started to fall in love with it and how he started to prepare training sessions.

"I'd get an opportunity to practice that with the 18s in the afternoon and it was something I wasn't that good at, and I felt uncomfortable at times.

"I was influenced by Mikel, but then I had to learn how to teach. I had to learn how to get that across, how to plan a session and how to get the outcomes that you wanted.

"I played under some good coaches and was quite good at understanding what a coach wants, but I never dived into 'why is he asking me to do that?' Mikel really made that clear and I was lucky enough to have a relationship where I could say, 'well, why do you want that?' And he was open enough to share it with me."

Not only did his former club Arsenal become English champions, but Wilshere gained extra satisfaction as he had coached defender Myles Lewis-Skelly, winger Ethan Nwaneri and midfielder Max Dowman during his time at the club's academy.

Wilshere was only 16 when he made his Arsenal debut, and Dowman was 15 when he first played for the Gunners senior team, with Wilshere spotting his talent early on.

"Max played for my 18s team when he was 13," added Wilshere. "I remember calling my dad because I played for the 18s when I was 14. I was like, 'was 13 too young?'

"In the first game we could clearly see that he was ready for it. And I remember calling my dad and saying, 'you need to come watch this kid'. My dad did, and my dad's very biased, as you could imagine. But even he said, 'he's better than you'."

Wilshere, who is aiming to guide Luton to promotion to the Championship this season, felt one of his managerial strengths was being able to warn his young players of the perils of professional football.

Early in his career he had been pictured drinking and smoking, leading to criticism from then Arsenal boss Arsene Wenger, but Wilshere said he learned from the experience and passes that knowledge on to his players.

"Yes, I made mistakes, but I also reflect on that," said Wilshere, who also played for Bolton, Bournemouth, West Ham and Danish side AGF. "I had a manager that had high standards and he let me know that he was disappointed, but he also gave me another chance.

"You educate them, you let them know there's a line and there's things they can't do. But also give them another chance. I believe in that."

Wilshere's man-management skills were shown when he delivered a passionate half-time team talk,, external which then went viral on social media, as Luton trailed Reading 3-1 on the opening day of this season, only to recover and clinch a dramatic 4-3 win.

"You have to build that relationship with the players," said Wilshere. "Players also want to have high standards. They want to be held accountable. Ever since day one, they've been all-in with what we've been trying to do.

"My idea is you have to work really, really hard. I want to give the players clarity in every single moment. I'd like to think I'm really hard-working, you have to be.

"You have to have a big love for the game because it takes over your life, which I do. Then if you have that blend and try and make it enjoyable for the players, there will be challenges along the way, but you're on the right path."

title: The student playing in La Liga: Introvert Rodri's unique rise to top
description: Rodri is already playing a key role at Barcelona after turning down Real Madrid this summer. Guillem Balague looks at his journey so far.
fullText:
Rodri never wanted to be interesting.

While a generation of players build personal brands and chase clicks, the Barcelona and Spain midfielder stays away from social media and avoids the spotlight, talking about tactics the way other players talk about cars.

He is, by his own admission, an introvert who happens to control football games for a living.

And it has been some career so far.

The 30-year-old won 12 major trophies with Man City and helped Spain to European Championship and World Cup successes.

On Saturday, he insisted his successes with Man City could not be taken away from them after the club were found guilty of breaking the majority of the 115 financial rules they were accused of breaching by the Premier League. City are set to appeal against the ruling.

He also won the Ballon d'Or in 2024 and is in contention to win it for a second time in October, a rare achievement for a holding midfielder.

From a Connecticut summer camp through a Castellon lecture hall to a Champions League final, Rodri has shown the willingness to absorb whatever the environment demands, understand why it is being asked of him - and get on with it.

Understanding his temperament and character is also the starting point for understanding why Barcelona, not Real Madrid, is where his career has turned next after leaving Man City in the summer.

Rodri believes in Man City's 'innocence'

Rodri's game was shaped by an education system that treats football intelligence as something to be taught and moulded.

Spanish academies function on the idea that a coach is a teacher first, and Rodri absorbed that from a young age. But he also came out of his comfort zone very early.

At 14, his father wanted him to spend a year at an American high school, but a season in Villarreal's youth ranks made that impossible, so the family found a compromise: a summer camp deep in the Connecticut woods.

That stay left him with the fluent, American-tinged English his Manchester City team-mates would later tease him about, and it is where he watched Spain win the 2010 World Cup, alone by a lake, thousands of miles from home.

His learning accelerated after being released by Atletico Madrid as a teenager, as his body had not caught up with his footballing brain.

Villarreal picked him up, and there the two strands of his life - football and study - ran in parallel. He moved to Castellon, the biggest city near Villarreal, at 17, and enrolled at university to study business administration.

He combined training in the morning with lectures in the afternoon. He cycled to training and lived among students who had no idea their quiet classmate would soon be starting in La Liga.

When he appeared on television one evening, his flatmates realised the boy from accounting class wore the number six shirt for Villarreal. He has since called that period the best of his life.

The rest of his rise is well known. Atletico brought him back in 2018 under Diego Simeone, who sharpened his intensity and competitiveness.

A year later, Manchester City paid his 70m euro release clause, and Guardiola turned him into arguably the finest holding midfielder of his generation.

There were setbacks, including a Champions League final defeat by Chelsea in 2021 that left him unable to speak to his own family afterwards. Two years later came the redemption, the goal that won City the Champions League in 2023.

That goal changed the story of his career. The Euros with Spain came and the Ballon d'Or followed, along with the World Cup title and MVP award that preceded his move to Barcelona this summer.

And you get the feeling his story is far from finished.

Rodri has been open about how seriously he took Real Madrid's interest in him this summer.

Speaking to Spanish sports radio station COPE, he said the club behaved impeccably and pursued him properly from the first approach.

He spoke to many in and around the club, and admitted the warmth of those conversations made his eventual decision harder.

New manager Jose Mourinho communicated his footballing idea clearly and what he wanted from Rodri personally, and that approach appealed to him.

Inside Real, the sense that Rodri was the player they needed went well beyond the coach.

Several figures at the club still regard him as the profile the squad is missing now, a controlling midfielder capable of dictating tempo in a way nobody currently on the books quite replicates.

The scale of Mourinho's pursuit reflected a genuine conviction that Rodri was required. Madrid have not gone out and found an alternative version of what he would have given them, so the gap the midfielder would have filled remains a gap.

Rodri's reasons for turning that interest down was footballing rather than personal.

His decision came down to where he could grow and contribute most, a project built around a squad full of young players, many of whom he knew already, and who fitted the way he understands the game.

It was a decision about which team needed what he offers, and where he could make the biggest difference.

Rodri is a footballing encyclopaedia and, many would argue, the best defensive midfielder in the world.

There are few better when it comes to positional play, and he is one of the very best because of what he does himself and what he brings out in his team-mates.

Without the ball, both in the press and when dropping back, he gives that sense of security in front of the defence, especially in those moments when Barcelona lose the ball.

But he is also outstanding with the ball because he distributes it quickly and always chooses the right route. You can see all that in every Barcelona game.

His arrival has been described inside the club as one of the most significant developments of recent years on and off the pitch - playing in all but one match of Barcelona's perfect start to the campaign.

For a squad that lost several senior voices in recent seasons, Rodri's experience in high-pressure moments has added a stability that had been missing.

He has taken on an informal mentoring role with the club's academy graduates, several of whom already regard him as a reference point.

He explains rather than simply demonstrates, an instinct that has surprised the coaching staff as much as his football has.

He does not wear the captain's armband, and probably will not for some time, but inside the dressing room many already talk about him as a captain in everything but title.

Boss Hansi Flick made clear from day one that Barcelona had signed a type of midfielder they did not have, but also a reference point for a squad in the middle of rebuilding.

His partnership with Pedri has emerged as one of the more encouraging signs, as there were doubts about it.

The two combine naturally, managing tempo and sharing the responsibility for circulating the ball. Flick sees them capable of controlling matches through positioning, possession and reading of the game rather than athleticism.

Asked to compare Flick with Guardiola, Rodri was unambiguous: they are nothing alike.

He has spoken about arriving at Barcelona expecting rondos and possession drills, only to be met with days of gruelling physical work in the gym.

Guardiola trusted competition to build match sharpness. Flick has taken a different route with the players who arrived later in pre-season, working them hard from the outset.

And as you would expect from his CV and personality, Rodri has adapted to it rather than resisted it.

title: Joker persona helps Cong 'feel the fear' in opponents
description: Wang Cong dismisses critics who say she she is not deserving of facing Natalia Silva for the flyweight world title at UFC 332 on Saturday.
fullText:
Before Wang Cong faces off with her opponents, she dyes her hair green, paints her face white and draws a bright red grin from cheek to cheek.

Fans may assume Cong is paying tribute to Batman's notorious arch-enemy the Joker, but the Chinese fighter says her persona is rooted in the joker playing card that inspired the comic-book villain.

The 34-year-old, who is on a four-fight win streak, says she can "feel the fear" in her opponents when she wears the face paint.

On Saturday at UFC 332 in Salt Lake City, Cong will be hoping she can invoke the same emotions in Brazilian Natalia Silva, when the pair fight for the vacant flyweight world title.

"It means the most powerful card, so I want to be the most powerful," Cong tells BBC Sport.

"When I have paint on I feel crazy. It makes me perform better, it inspires me. There's not much different between paint and no paint, this is my true personality."

Cong has bewildered opponents at weigh-ins while wearing the face paint, and says she even adopts the Joker alias when using social media messaging back home in China.

She tossed an imaginary coin and pretended to shoot a gun before her fight against Gabriella Fernandes in 2024, while in July she bizarrely gifted Tracy Cortez a pack of fake eyelashes before the pair's flyweight encounter.

Cong laughs as she reveals Silva can expect a "surprise" of her own before their fight at the Delta Centre, although she then turns serious as she pays tribute to her opponent.

Silva, 29, enters the contest on a 14-fight win streak across different promotions and is the favourite to capture the vacant title after Valentina Shevchenko was forced to vacate the belt last month through injury.

"She's an incredible fighter, an eight-fight win streak in UFC, beaten three former champions, she has amazing footwork, distance control and kicks," adds Cong.

Silva, who is number one in the UFC's flyweight rankings, was set to face Shevchenko for the belt before the bout was cancelled, so was expected to challenge for the vacant title.

Some fans were surprised that sixth-ranked Cong was chosen for the title fight however, and she admits she felt the same way.

"To be honest I was a little bit surprised but if you see the rankings, the girls ranked higher than me have either a fight booked or they have just fought," said Cong.

"I'm on a four-win streak so that makes sense."

The fight represents the first women's main event in the UFC since Mackenzie Dern beat Amanda Ribas is January 2025.

The last time two women headlined one of the UFC's flagship numbered events was when Amanda Nunes defeated in June 2023.

Cong says it's "meaningful" to be flying the flag for women's MMA after a period of under representation in the UFC, and is excited for the opportunities her success could create in China.

If Cong wins, she will become only the second Chinese UFC champion after former strawweight title holder Zhang Weili.

"MMA is my final transition in my combat sports career. I think my success will encourage more athletes to be brave and try mixed martial arts in China," said Cong.

The event has received criticism from some fans on social media, who instead called for the main event to feature fighters such as Jiri Prochazka, Ciryl Gane and Alex Pereira.

When asked if Cong has a message for her critics, she was concise in her response.

"I've got nothing to say right now. After my fight I think they will shut up," she said.

title: Verstappen takes first 2026 pole ahead of Hamilton
description: Max Verstappen takes his and Red Bull's first pole position of 2026 with an imperious performance in qualifying at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.
fullText:
Max Verstappen took his and Red Bull's first pole position of 2026 with an imperious performance in qualifying at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, ahead of Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton.

Verstappen, whose last pole and victory was at the season finale in Abu Dhabi in 2026, was 0.298 seconds quicker than Hamilton after topping all three sessions of qualifying.

Red Bull's Isack Hadjar was third fastest but has a five-place grid penalty, which will promote runaway championship leader Kimi Antonelli to third place.

The Italian's closest rival, team-mate George Russell, could manage only eighth fastest.

Ferrari's Charles Leclerc was fifth fastest, ahead of the McLarens of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri.

Fernando Alonso, fresh from confirming he will stay in F1 for at least another year in 2027, gave Aston Martin their best qualifying position of the year with 12th place, behind Alpine's Pierre Gasly, Audi's Gabriel Bortoleto and Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson.

The second Aston Martin of Lance Stroll was 14th, split from Alonso by Williams' Carlos Sainz.

Red Bull introduced a aerodynamic upgrade at the last race in Azerbaijan, and it has proved to be a major step forward at the demanding Sepang track, hosting this race after it was postponed earlier in the year because of the war in the Middle East.

Verstappen has had a difficult year, struggling for pace and balance for much of it, but he is on a strong run of results after steady improvements to the car.

"Fantastic," he said. "We have been trying many grands prix to get pole, sometimes a bit closer than others. But to finally get it from where we started the season, pretty incredible."

Hamilton's position on the front row revives memories of their bitter title battle in 2021, when the seven-time champion was at Mercedes, and whets appetites for the grand prix on Sunday.

Hamilton said: "It's so hot here. That's made it a massive challenge for the cars, the tyres, the mechanics in the garage.

"Because the tyres are sliding, it's so hard to find a good balance and we made one change and we finally hit the sweet spot."

Mercedes have brought their first major upgrade since the Canadian Grand Prix in June, but it has not proved the step forward hoped.

Unusally, Antonelli went into qualifying with only four new sets of soft tyres rather than the usual five and compromised his programme by having his first lap in second session deleted for going beyond track limits.

That meant he had to use another set of tyres in the session, which left him only one for the final shootout.

He went out in the middle of the session, after the others did their first runs, and ended up with a time 0.501secs from pole, much further away than Mercedes would have hoped.

Antonelli said: "It's a shame because with only one set, big pressure. I did what I could but with another set we could have fought for front row. Not P1, because Max was too quick today."

But he fared better than Russell, who was lacking pace compared to his team-mate all day, and ended up 0.240secs off Antonelli.

The Briton said: "It's the most demanding circuit on the tyres, so we don't know exactly why we didn't have the pace. From Friday it was clear we weren't on the pace of the Red Bulls and we haven't really progressed. The others have caught up and overtaken [us]."

It was also a difficult day for McLaren, who were tipped by Russell as the potential frontrunners going into the weekend because of their car's strong recent performances on tracks that share characteristics with this one.

But they lacked pace all weekend and Norris could manage only a best lap of 0.627secs off the pace.

For Aston Martin, though, this was confirmation that changes they have made to their car in recent races have borne fruit.

They struggled in Italy and Azerbaijan because their Honda engine remains the worst in the field, despite two recent upgrades.

But on a track where power sensitivity is lower, the improvements to the chassis made in terms of aerodynamics and weight since the summer added up.

A lap by Alonso that was 1.524secs off the pace is by far their strongest performance of the year, and a suggestion that the veteran's faith they could step forward significantly in 2027 has some foundation.

"It was definitely one the best qualifying of the year," Alonso said. "1.5secs to top of Q2, so smallest margin. It seems this circuit is a little better for our package and let's see tomorrow if we can take advantage of this."

title: Lewandowski, 38, hits hat-trick in 6-0 Poland win
description: Robert Lewandowski, 38, scores a hat-trick in the Nations League and Edin Dzeko plays his final game for Bosnia-Herzegovina.
fullText:
Robert Lewandowski scored a hat-trick as Poland thrashed 10-man Romania 6-0 in the Nations League.

After Tottenham defender Radu Dragusin, who is on loan at Fiorentina, was sent off in the 22nd minute, Romania were dismantled in Warsaw.

Lewandowski opened the scoring from the penalty spot and doubled the lead early in the second half.

An own goal and strikes from Piotr Zielinski and Jan Bednarek followed before 38-year-old Lewandowski completed his seventh international hat-trick.

The former Barcelona striker has scored 92 international goals.

Poland are third in Group B4, while Romania stay fourth.

Gheorghe Hagi, in his second spell in charge, became the first Romania manager to lose his first three competitive matches.

In the same group there were emotional scenes as Edin Dzeko retired from international football following Bosnia-Herzegovina's 1-1 draw at home to Sweden.

The ex-Manchester City forward, 40, found the net late in the first half but the goal was disallowed as the ball went out of play in the build-up.

Fireworks went off after 11 minutes to celebrate the number 11 on his 152nd international appearance, and he was given a standing ovation when he was substituted after 62 minutes in Zenica.

The celebrations continued after the match with an official ceremony, a guard of honour and a drone show displaying messages of thanks to Dzeko, who was showered with soft toys from the crowd during a lap of honour.

Arsenal striker Viktor Gyokeres put Sweden in front before Kerim Alajbegovic equalised for Bosnia-Herzegovina.

Kevin de Bruyne scored twice as Belgium beat Turkey 3-0 to move up to second in Group A1.

The 35-year-old Napoli midfielder scored a goal in each half before Romelu Lukaku completed the scoring.

Liverpool defender Milos Kerkez scored the only goal as Hungary beat Georgia in Budapest to claim their first Nations League win of the campaign.

Hungary are third in Group B2, three points behind leaders Northern Ireland.

title: Kim wins Asian Games gold to secure military exemption
description: Golfer Tom Kim wins gold at the Asian Games to secure an exemption from mandatory service in South Korea's military.
fullText:
-18 T Kim (Kor); -15 K Higa (Jpn), W Ding (Chi), S Kaewkanjana (Tha); -11 W-H Wang (Tpe)

Tom Kim won gold at the Asian Games to secure an exemption from mandatory service in South Korea's military.

The 24-year-old led going into the final round and produced a brilliant six-under-par 64 to finish 18 under and claim victory by three strokes.

There were signs of nerves with a bogey on the 17th but, after five birdies and an eagle prior to that, Kim had the margin for error and tapped in for par on the last before letting out a roar, his relief clear to see.

Able-bodied South Korean males are usually required to undertake between 18 and 21 months of military service before the age of 28.

However, the government rewards Asian Games champions and Olympic medal-winners of any colour with a service exemption bar basic training, which lasts less than a month.

Athletes who have previously secured the exemption include former Tottenham footballer Son Heung-min, who served for only three weeks in 2020 having won the Asian Games with his country two years earlier.

Kim rushed from the Presidents Cup in the United States to tee off at the Kasugai Country Club in Japan, having to manage on just six hours of sleep and a 14-hour time difference.

His efforts were worth it as the world number 32 can now continue his career, in which he has already won four PGA Tour titles and triumphed at the Scottish Open in July, with minimal disruption.

Kim had previously come close to securing an exemption at the Paris Olympics in 2024, finishing day one tied for third before ultimately finishing eighth.

However, his compatriot SH Kim, 28, missed out on a military exemption as South Korea could only win silver in the team event, alongside Tom Kim and Mun Do-yeob, who has already completed his service.

title: Too quiet for too long, can McGinn recapture best for Scotland?
description: Fifth in the all-time scoring chart for Scotland and closing in on 100 caps, John McGinn could do with finding his best stuff again, writes Tom English.
fullText:
In Skopje these past few days it's been difficult to figure out the most devout people - the local followers of the city's most sacred daughter, Mother Teresa, or the arriving Scots and their most cherished son, Saint John McGinn.

Faith in the blessed one is absolute (and the same goes for Teresa). Raise a critical note and you could be shot down in flames. Point out that McGinn's talismanic excellence has been on the wane in international football for a little while now and you're liable to reap a whirlwind.

This is a weekend when Andy Robertson wins his 100th cap, but McGinn isn't far behind.

After Saturday night he'll be on 92, third on the all-time appearance list while currently sitting in fifth in the all-time scoring chart, one behind the immortal Lawrie Reilly.

There is something to be said, though, and you say it with the hesitancy of a bomb disposal expert approaching a suspect device. For Scotland, McGinn could do with finding his best stuff again.

When he arrives to chat at the Todor Proeski Stadium in Skopje he is compelling when talking about his form, his confidence, his status as inspiration of the team and whatever pressure that comes with it.

"The nature of the beast is, at club and country, you have a lot of responsibility, a lot of weight on your shoulders," he said. "When you do something well, you're the best thing since sliced bread. When you don't have a great couple of games, or you're not producing assists, or you make a poor pass in a pivotal moment of the game, you're automatically not good enough.

"It's the nature of being my age (he'll be 32 later in the month). It's the nature of competing with Scotland and with Aston Villa. I take the praise with a big smile. Any criticism that comes, it's just part of it."

McGinn's influence for his country has probably reduced from the mighty highs of before. None of the pride and passion and phenomenal work-rate has gone, but the game-defining moments have not been there, save for the odd glimpse.

Pocognoli not feeling pressure for first Scotland win

Robertson's Scotland career in numbers as 100th cap looms

Haiti, and the double deflection, sticks out, but beyond that, McGinn has been too quiet for too long. It's unfair to saddle him with the expectation of being superman every time he plays, but he's the one who fans look to, his is the name they chant in good times and in bad.

His last Scotland goal before Haiti at the World Cup was coming up for two years ago.

Opproprium will rein down for the mere mention of him being under pressure to deliver, of course. Being McGinn, he could dominate and score in Skopje, but a reminder of his talent is overdue.

You ask if he feels, as a 91-cap colossus, undroppable. "No, no. I'm certainly not undroppable, " he replied. "I remember Steve Clarke put me on the bench and I had absolutely no issue with that.

"I don't think anyone in the squad is undroppable. It's the challenge to anyone coming into the squad and I encourage that challenge.

"The competition is always there, whether that's someone who's 20, 21 or in their 30s. The best players will play for Scotland. If the manager said to me, 'You're on the bench, I need you for five minutes, ten minutes, zero minutes or 90-plus', we're here to represent Scotland.

"The thing that's made us so successful over the years is that it doesn't matter if you play for Aston Villa, Motherwell, Hibs, St Mirren, anyone. You represent Scotland and at the end of the day the best team will take to the pitch.

"If that's a team without me in it, I'll be the biggest Scotland supporter on the bench."

What keeps him driving on? He's quick to answer. "What keeps me going is how I felt on that first night (his 2016 debut) against Denmark - the pride, the emotion. When you're picked to play for your country, you never know when it's going to be your last, so you don't take it for granted.

"Quite possibly tomorrow night, you never know. It could be the last time you're chosen."

McGinn, of course, has glorious history and iconic status with St Mirren and Hibs, but at Villa something extra-special has happened. His status is now deeply rooted as a legend of the club. Talk to their fans and it's not an appraisal you get but a hagiography. Understandably.

McGinn (more than most others) was the one who got them out of the Championship in 2019, the one who kept them in the Premier League in 2020, the one who dragged them from 17th to 11th to 14th to 7th to 4th in the English top flight, the one who helped bring Champions League football, the one who captained them and scored for them when winning a European trophy last season, the one who broke their European goalscoring record.

McGinn was one of the ones who stayed. Jack Grealish didn't, Douglas Luiz didn't, Ollie Watkins didn't, Emi Martinez didn't, Youri Tielemans didn't.

The best Villa captain since Dennis Mortimer, some say. Given that Mortimer was leader of the iconic league winning team of 1981 and the European Cup winning side of 1982 then that's some compliment.

What makes a legend, somebody asked recently in a Villa discussion. "Humility", "determination", "tenacity", "leadership", "longevity", "success." One club diehard wrote that they've had loads of players in recent decades who tick some of those boxes but it takes a special individual to tick all of them - "and McGinn does."

As one observer put it: "He's unquestionably ahead of any other player we've had this century and surpasses some of the legends from the last one, too." Another said that he fully expects his infant son to say to him in later life: "What was it like watching John McGinn?"

He's too long in the tooth now to be overly influenced by praise or flak. "If I was younger, I would have been straight on Instagram or straight on Twitter," he added. "Everyone's entitled to their opinion, but at the end of the day, you keep your head down, you keep working hard.

"If you go through a barren spell or you go through a spell where you're not doing too well, you need to find that inner self-belief, which I feel like I have. The older you get, you learn how to manage tough moments better. They get worse, though.

"The lows get lower and the highs become less high. But you certainly deal with it a lot better when you're older. When you're younger, it completely consumes you and you try and work too hard to come out of what could potentially be a difficult moment. But I feel as if I'm managing those times well.

"As you get older, you think, 'Oh, can I keep doing this?' But it certainly makes the good days a lot better. You know after a game like Switzerland, do you turn the telly on? No. Do you listen to radio reports? Nope. But if it's 3-0 to Scotland, I would be lying if I said I wouldn't listen to some of it."

The prospect of following in Robertson's footsteps is an enormous incentive. Eight to go after North Macedonia.

More fireworks to come, you hope. Compared to the huge moments in past seasons, McGinn might be in a bit of an international lull right now, but is there a single soul out there who thinks he's done with the heroics? In the tartan-clad city of Teresa, few, you fancy, have lost belief.

description:

Pike was given a death sentence in 1996 after being convicted of killing her classmate, Colleen Slemmer, in an attack she carried out with her then boyfriend. fullText:
The failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee on Wednesday has added new fuel to the longstanding debate over the death penalty in the United States. It has also drawn new scrutiny to the question of whether lethal injection, the nation's primary method of execution for the past 40 years, is truly a "more humane" alternative to other ways of putting someone to death.

Pike was given a death sentence in 1996 after being convicted of killing her classmate, Colleen Slemmer, in an attack she carried out with her then boyfriend. After 30 years on death row, and a last-minute legal battle that temporarily delayed her execution, Pike was scheduled to be put to death on Wednesday night.

However, the two doses of pentobarbital she was given proved not to be fatal. According to witnesses, Pike remained alive and snored loudly for 40 minutes after the drugs were administered. Eventually, the execution was called off and she was taken to the hospital for treatment.

Pike's attorney Randy Spivey reported Thursday afternoon that she was in critical condition and receiving "life-saving care." She was unconscious and placed on a ventilator in the hospital, according to a filing by her legal team on Friday.

Spivey admonished the state for going forward with lethal injection despite his warnings ahead of time that a blood-clotting disorder called thrombocytosis "would cause her to suffer an agonizing death." Pike's attorneys had asked the courts to permit her to die by hanging, but the request was denied.

"The state of Tennessee has shown once again that they are not capable of carrying out an execution consistent with basic human dignity," he said. "Last night was not just inefficient, it was cruel and it was torturous. It was also predictable."

Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee suspended all other executions in the state and called for a "comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred."

Pike is the first person in modern U.S. history to survive the administration of lethal injection drugs, according to the nonprofit Death Penalty Information Center. Seven other attempted lethal injections have failed, but in each case, the execution was called off due to difficulties finding a vein to administer the drugs.

The doctor who administered Pike's failed execution was reportedly involved in the state's previous botched lethal injection earlier this year.

Lethal injection has been by far the most common form of execution in the United States since it was first introduced in the early 1980s, thanks largely to the view that it provides the quiet, non-violent death that other methods do not. But Pike is just one of many examples that contradict that belief, showing that lethal injections can sometimes be complex, error-prone and at times cause extreme suffering.

For centuries, executing someone inherently meant subjecting them to a violent death, either through hanging, the electric chair, firing squad or the gas chamber.

It wasn't until the 1970s, in the wake of a Supreme Court ruling barring "cruel and unusual punishment," that states began seeking less violent methods of executing prisoners.

The first law legalizing lethal injection was introduced by an Oklahoma lawmaker who opposed the death penalty entirely, but felt the state should at least find an alternative to what he called the "dirty deed" of electrocuting a person to death. Supporters of legalizing lethal injection described it as a "more humane" alternative to electrocution. The first lethal injection was carried out in 1982 in Texas. Injection soon became the primary method of execution throughout the country.

Nearly 90% of the 1,693 executions carried out in the United States over the past 50 years have been by lethal injection. Lethal injection is the primary execution method in 25 of the 27 states that allow the death penalty. Only nine states use the electric chair or gas chamber.

For decades, the primary approach was to inject the condemned person with a three-drug cocktail designed to put them to sleep, paralyze them and then stop their heart. In theory, this would mean that they died without experiencing any pain.

But the procedure is also much more complex than some other execution methods, which increases the chances that something can go wrong. Between 1982 and 2010, there were 75 botched injection executions that featured "unan­tic­i­pat­ed prob­lems" or "unnec­es­sary agony for the pris­on­er," according to research by Amherst College professor Austin Sarat. Lethal injections face complications at a significantly higher rate than any other execution method.

There's also growing evidence that lethal injection may not provide a peaceful death even when everything appears to go right. In 2020, NPR looked at the autopsies of more than 200 people who had died by lethal injection. It found that the overwhelming majority of their bodies showed signs that the prisoners likely endured what one medical expert described as "a cir­cus of suf­fer­ing" before dying that wasn't visible to witnesses.

More than 20 pharmaceutical companies have also refused to have their products used in executions, which has left states struggling to find the drugs they need to perform lethal injections. In some cases, they have experimented with unproven alternatives, with disastrous results.

An Oklahoma prisoner named Michael Lee Wilson said he could feel his "whole body burning" as he was being executed using a controversial drug cocktail in 2014. There have also been instances of prisoners gasping for air, heaving and coughing, convulsing and being subjected to "three hours of pain" before finally dying.

Mounting awareness of the shortcomings of lethal injection has led to calls for the revival of execution methods that had previously been largely abandoned.

"While there should be a thorough review of what happened and why the process failed, the answer is simple: bring back the electric chair and deliver justice for these victims swiftly," Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the current GOP nominee to become Tennessee's next governor, wrote on social media Thursday.

Some legal scholars have made the case that firing squads, for all of their brutality, may be the least inhumane way to put someone to death. That includes liberal Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor, who wrote in a 2015 opinion that "such visible yet relatively painless violence may be vastly preferable to an excruciatingly painful death hidden behind a veneer of medication."

Early last year, a convicted murderer in South Carolina named Brad Sigmon became the first person to die by firing squad in the U.S. in more than 15 years. The state carried out two more firing squad executions before the end of the year. All three inmates chose to die by firing squad. Sigmon's lawyers told the Associated Press that he chose to die by firing squad to avoid the "monstrous" results of a botched lethal injection.

Five other states also allow the use of firing squads. That includes Idaho, which recently made it the state's primary method of execution. The Department of Justice announced in April that it would add the firing squad to its list of potential execution methods in federal death penalty cases.

Another novel execution method, nitrogen gas, was used for the first time in Alabama in 2024.

Though research suggests these other methods are less prone to error than lethal injections, there are still many examples of how things can go horribly wrong.

Past electrocutions have involved inmates catching fire or surviving multiple waves of shocks before dying.

Mikal Mahdi, a man who was killed by a firing squad last year, appeared to suffer tremendously before dying. He reportedly cried out after being shot, groaned twice and continued to breathe for more than a minute before falling motionless. A later autopsy showed that only two of the three bullets that were fired at Mahdi hit him, and neither of them struck his heart as intended.

The first person executed with nitrogen gas spent two minutes making "thrashing spasms and seizure-like movements" before falling still and wasn't declared dead until 10 minutes later. A later execution using the same method took more than 30 minutes to take effect and involved the inmate taking a long series of "heaving breaths."

It's unclear whether Wednesday's botched lethal injection will lead Tennessee to consider other execution methods in the future.

title: Trump announces one-time $90 payment for over 20 million Medicare seniors
description:
President Donald Trump said the US government will send a one-time $90 payment to more than 20 million ‌Americans enrolled in Medicare, a health insurance program for the elderly, ‌to help offset the cost of their monthly medical insurance premiums. 
   Trump said on social media late ​on Friday the payments will come from the Medicare Improvement Fund, which he said was given $2 billion by Congress to improve the Medicare fee-for-service program. 
   The announcement is the latest in a series of financial promises the Republican leader has made to ‌voters heading into the November ⁠midterm elections where control of Congress is at stake. 
   Trump's Republican Party currently has a narrow majority in both the Senate ⁠and the House of Representatives but his approval rating has been low over his handling of the high cost of living for Americans during the US-Israeli war on ​Iran that ​has spiked oil and gas prices. 
   The White ​House released some details of ‌Trump's plan on its website, saying most eligible seniors will receive the payment in the form of a direct deposit of $90 in early October.
fullText:
WASHINGTON, Oct 2 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump said the US government will send a one-time $90 payment to more than 20 million ‌Americans enrolled in Medicare, a health insurance program for the elderly, ‌to help offset the cost of their monthly medical insurance premiums.

Trump said on social media late ​on Friday the payments will come from the Medicare Improvement Fund, which he said was given $2 billion by Congress to improve the Medicare fee-for-service program.

The announcement is the latest in a series of financial promises the Republican leader has made to ‌voters heading into the November ⁠midterm elections where control of Congress is at stake.

Trump's Republican Party currently has a narrow majority in both the Senate ⁠and the House of Representatives but his approval rating has been low over his handling of the high cost of living for Americans during the US-Israeli war on ​Iran that ​has spiked oil and gas prices.

The White ​House released some details of ‌Trump's plan on its website, saying most eligible seniors will receive the payment in the form of a direct deposit of $90 in early October.

Those without direct deposit will receive a check, also sent in early October, to the mailing address they have registered with Medicare, the White House said.

Last month, Trump proposed sending $5,000 ‌checks to all adult citizens if the ​Republicans keep control of the House and Senate ​in the midterms, though analysts, economists ​and even some Republicans in Congress reacted with skepticism to ‌the plan.

The Trump administration is also ​separately sending $500 payments to ​nearly 1 million Americans in a move that strategists say could potentially influence some election races.

The White House says those payments were a refund ​for what it describes ‌as excessive fees charged to people who purchased health insurance through ​the Affordable Care Act.

title: The Prediction: USC Trojans
description: The UWDP Staff makes their predictions for a road tilt in the Coliseum!
fullText:
This week, the Huskies go on the road to the Coliseum to face the #18 USC Trojans, with both programs looking to right their ships as they head deeper into Big Ten play! Our staff has their predictions below!

There seems to be a belief in Vegas (or the betting public) that Washington has another gear they haven't hit yet. The Dawgs are 0-4 ATS because they just haven't scored enough points to beat the spreads, which have favored them in every game so far. This one looks like more of the same- how many points will UW need to score to realistically stay within single digits of one of the better offense's in the country?

Sure, if you want to pick nits, you can point out that USC's receiver room is not fully healthy, which contributed to Jayden Maiava's more pedestrian output against Oregon. You can also note that USC's defense has been quite poor, allowing 30+ to each of Rutgers, Louisiana, and Oregon (mostly without Dante Moore). On the other hand, I don't expect the defense to be meaningfully worse than Washington St or Utah St, both of whom gave UW plenty of problems. I could see an offensive breakthrough for UW if Jedd Fisch calls 10 more designed QB runs for Demond Williams, or if Williams does find that higher gear that has been missing this season. Those changes could get UW within 10 points, but I have not seen anything this season to make me think those changes are coming.

Given what USC is as a program, or at least perceived to be, it feels like this game is always one of three things for the Huskies.

An opportunity to prove they can perform under the bright light of national television (both CFP appearances featured battles with USC along the way)

A chance for a new coach to earn or retain high placement in the West Coast pecking order (Sark beat USC Year 1, Petersen Year 2, DeBoer Year 2, Fisch Year 1)

A potential turning point for the season

We're currently at #3 after Washington's slow start, which isn't reflected in its 3-1 (0-1 Big Ten) record. The Huskies need to find a groove offensively. Though narratives suggest USC's defense is horrid, the Trojans have a lot of talent on the defensive line, and the Huskies' offensive line has struggled. That is not a recipe for success. However, I think Jedd Fisch will make an adjustment and utilize Demond Williams' legs more, because the Huskies don't have a chance unless Williams is put in designed runs, or at least RPOs. I don't expect Washington's running game to come to life in this game. Last time UW traveled to USC it captured a 52-42 victory in an instant classic. That game led to the firing of USC defensive coordinator Alex Grinch, as a misalignment led to explosive runs by ex-Husky running back Dillon Johnson. If USC loses this game, calls for Lincoln Riley's job will grow deafening, as it will feature consecutive losses to foes from the Pacific Northwest. This game is tough to call. My heart says the Huskies will find a way to win, as they've been successful against USC in recent years. My brain tells me there is nothing the Huskies have shown me to suggest they'll win this game. I'm going to trust the brain, but hope the heart is right.

This week, it's a battle between 2 programs at their nadir in terms of vibes. On one side, you have the Huskies, joined at the hip to a quarterback who has regressed, if anything, and an offense that is not physical enough in pass protection or in the run game. That, with a defense that has played ever sloppily and carelessly throughout the weeks doesn't instill a ton of confidence.

However, USC has its own issues, despite a ton of talent in Jaiden Maiva and King Miller among others. Lincoln Riley notably can't figure out defense, for one. Gary Patterson's unit has weaknesses in the back end that the Huskies, if they can exploit them, can ride them to an upset win. That is a big if, as we don't know how Demond or the line will hold up against a defensive line that is pretty stout. But if he can, and we can get receivers open, we may end up winning this one. As far as the rushing attack, I don't have faith in the running backs, or Jedd getting Demond involved on designed runs. So it falls to the pass game, and the big question is: can Demond live up to the preseason hype, just a little bit? I don't know if he can.

Straight Up: Washington–0, USC–3

Against the Spread: Washington–1, USC–2

Average Score: USC–35.333, Washington–21.33

Let us know your prediction in the comments below! Go Dawgs!

title: Yankees’ Gerrit Cole Ties CC Sabathia in MLB History
description: The New York Yankees made the call that folks weren’t sure they would make. Gerrit Cole is going to start Game 1 of the ALDS on Saturday against the Tampa Bay Rays. Despite struggles late in the season, Cole will get the ball for the game in Tropicana Field that could be crucial for the […] The post Yankees’ Gerrit Cole Ties CC Sabathia in MLB History appeared first on HEAVY.
fullText:
The New York Yankees made the call that folks weren't sure they would make.

Gerrit Cole is going to start Game 1 of the ALDS on Saturday against the Tampa Bay Rays.

Despite struggles late in the season, Cole will get the ball for the game in Tropicana Field that could be crucial for the Yankees to win in what is just a best-of-five series.

The Cole Train comes to Tampa for ALDS Game 1 🚂#RepBX pic.twitter.com/uTSBdY0ba3

— New York Yankees (@Yankees) October 2, 2026

Whether or not the Yankees should be starting Cole will only reveal itself on Saturday.

For now, there is a cool bit of history.

Cole has a long history of starting Game 1 in postseason series.

This will be his ninth Game 1 start (if you also include the single-game Wild Card Series that used to exist).

That's tied for fifth-most all-time, according to MLB Network's Sarah Langs.

Tied with Cole with nine of these starts? CC Sabathia.

In fourth place on the all-time Game 1 starts list is Greg Maddux, who had 11.

There's a tie for second place: Both Clayton Kershaw and Jon Lester started 12 of these games.

And alone in first place, potentially for a long time: Justin Verlander, with 14.

This will be the 9th time Gerrit Cole starts Game 1 of a postseason series (including singular Wild Card Game), tying CC Sabathia for 5th-most all time, behind:

Justin Verlander: 14
 Jon Lester: 12
 Clayton Kershaw: 12
 Greg Maddux: 11 https://t.co/NgopsVMhCQ

— Sarah Langs (@SlangsOnSports) October 2, 2026

Cole finished the 2026 regular season with a 3.61 ERA. That's his worst mark since 2017.

To be fair, it's still a really quality number, but Cole did prove a bit homer-prone late in the year. He also had his lowest strikeout rate (9.3 per nine innings) since that 2017 season, as well.

Cole has been a great playoff pitcher in his career. He has a 2.77 ERA in the postseason.

In the Yankees' 2024 playoff run to the World Series, he had a 2.17 ERA in five games.

Cole's most recent Game 1 start was in Game 1 of the 2024 World Series. He allowed just one run in six innings.

Cole has once faced the Rays in an ALDS Game 1, as well. That was in 2020. He went 6.0 innings and allowed three runs, including two home runs — Randy Arozarena with the first one, and Ji-man Choi with the second.

That game clearly has no real bearing on what happens on Saturday. The Rays beat the Yankees for the AL East title. Now, the Yanks will try and avenge that by potentially winning the ALDS. Cole will have to set the tone on the mound.

title: Penguins F Andrei Kuzmenko switches jersey to No. 62 to honor father killed in bear attack in Russia
description: Pittsburgh Penguins forward Andrei Kuzmenko is changing his jersey number to 62 to honor his father Alexander, who died in a bear attack in Russia last week at age 62.
fullText:
Pittsburgh Penguins forward Andrei Kuzmenko is changing his jersey number to 62 to honor his father Alexander, who died in a bear attack in Russia last week at age 62.

Andrei Kuzmenko returned to practice with the Penguins on Friday for the first time since returning from his father's funeral in Moscow.

The 30-year-old Kuzmenko, who signed a one-year, $5 million contract with Pittsburgh over the summer, also offered a brief statement outlining his understanding of what happened to his dad while on a fishing trip in the Tyva section of Siberia.

"My father go permit fishing with friends, and he stayed in the water," Andrei Kuzmenko said. "And bear (stand) behind him and attack. And my father fight (the) bear one hour, 10 minutes and he still lived after two days."

Kuzmenko, who used to wear No. 10, added that his father's death was a "big shock." Kuzmenko also noted that his mother was born in 1962.

Pittsburgh plays Montreal in its home opener on Saturday.

title: Zack Of All Trades Tries To Get One More Win: In Court
description: Zack Gelof is one of those athletes who only has one speed: full bore ahead. It’s part of what makes him an elite athlete and at times it makes it difficult for him to stay on the field. But there is also a difference between playing with “reckless abandon” and having “no regard for your […]
fullText:
Zack Gelof is one of those athletes who only has one speed: full bore ahead. It's part of what makes him an elite athlete and at times it makes it difficult for him to stay on the field. But there is also a difference between playing with "reckless abandon" and having "no regard for your body," and hitting the ER because the other team's stadium operations executives had no regard for your body.

In July, 2017 the A's acquired Dustin Fowler from the New York Yankees as he was recovering from a serious knee injury, a rupture of his right patella tendon. In December, 2017, Fowler sued the Chicago White Sox, claiming negligence due to an unpadded, metal electrical box that was located in precisely the area where Fowler impacted the wall. Fowler's lawsuit settled for an undisclosed amount of cash.

Now comes Gelof's lawsuit filed against the Detroit Tigers after Gelof badly lacerated his leg on July 9 when his pursuit of a foul fly ball took him into the side wall — where instead of padding there was a stretch of metal wiring that sliced Gelof's knee like a Veg-O-Matic and kept him out of action for a month.

Some injuries are preventable and many aren't. Some mishaps are the result of foreseeable gross negligence and many are just plain bad luck. Stadium operators are obliged to notice clear safety hazards, and many hazards only reveal themselves when a fluky play exposes a formerly unknown truth.

The question in front of a judge or jury, first to be mediated by posturing attorneys, is whether Gelof's injury was caused by a negligence that anyone could have, and should have, reasonably foreseen. The law doesn't compensate you for bad luck like it does for bad faith.

Did the Tigers expressly have an obligation to put padding, or avoid putting a wire facing, in a part of the playing field a fielder might slide or crash into? Did Gelof have some obligation either to avoid going full tilt into a very visible wire structure or to notice the hazard during batting practice and bring it to someone's attention?

Separately there is the question of "damages" as the two sides haggle about the "value" of the case. Certainly there was appreciable pain and suffering — that much was clear at the time of the collision as well as the fact that Gelof could not take the field in a big league game for 32 days.

But he was also paid while on the IL and rehab assignments, so there was no loss of income there. His future value, and how this injury did or did not affect it, is a pretty subjective question, but we do know that Gelof put up a 116 wRC+ before the injury and a very similar 112 wRC+ after.

One thing is for sure: Fowler's case will be raised, by both sides, in conversations around Gelof's chances of prevailing in his lawsuit and the value of any settlement. Fowler created precedent that informs comparable cases. And once again, here is an outfielder who was racing into foul territory when he bludgeoned himself on an exposed and unforgiving barrier to his pursuit.

What do you think are the material facts in Gelof's case and who do they ultimately favor? In all likelihood this case, like the one before it, will settle and never go to trial and the settlement amount will not be made public. But if you were on a jury and were asked to rule on the merits, what information would most inform your verdict and what would that verdict look like? In the end, will Gelof get the 65th win of the season to bring vengeance upon the stadium where Oakland's season was ended 20 years prior?

title: Mizzou volleyball falls to Ole Miss in four-set road battle
description: Mizzou Volleyball loses SEC road opener.
fullText:
Mizzou volleyball and its road woes continued as the Tigers could not carry its momentum from its Southeastern Conference opener into Friday night, falling to Ole Miss 3-1 at the Gillom Center. The Tigers dropped the first two sets 25-20 and 25-22 before forcing a fourth set with a 25-20 victory, but Ole Miss closed the match with a 25-20 win in the fourth.

Paige Felder led Missouri offensively with 13 kills on 28 attacks, hitting .321 for the match. Grace O'Reilly added 11 kills and hit .192, while Kimani Johnson and Lydia Stahley each finished with seven kills. Lauren Larkin contributed five kills and hit .300 while adding two service aces.

The Tigers had opportunities early but struggled to consistently turn their attacks into points. Missouri hit .212 as a team with 45 kills and 20 errors, while Ole Miss finished with 47 kills and a .216 hitting percentage. The Rebels also held an advantage at the net, recording nine total blocks to Missouri's five.

Missouri opened the match with a strong offensive first set, hitting .435 with 12 kills and only two errors. Ole Miss, however, answered with 13 kills and a .346 hitting percentage to take the opening frame 25-20.

The second set became another back and forth battle, with Missouri producing 16 kills, its highest total of the match in a single set. Felder and Johnson each recorded four kills in the frame, but Ole Miss limited its mistakes with only one attack error and held off the Tigers 25-22.

Missouri responded in the third set by turning to its defense and forcing Ole Miss into mistakes. The Tigers held the Rebels to a .000 hitting percentage, with Ole Miss recording nine kills and nine errors. Missouri took advantage behind nine kills of its own, including multiple contributions from Felder, O'Reilly and Larkin, to extend the match.

The fourth set remained close before Ole Miss created separation late. Missouri committed eight attack errors in the frame and finished with its lowest offensive efficiency of the night, hitting .000 on 31 attempts. Ole Miss produced 10 kills and closed the match with a .065 hitting percentage to secure the 3-1 victory.

Ainoah Cruz anchored Missouri defensively with 19 digs, while Nina Mandovic recorded 21 assists. Sierra Dudley added 20 assists and five digs, giving the Tigers production from multiple spots throughout the match.

The loss gives Missouri its first SEC defeat of the season and leaves the Tigers needing to regroup quickly before their next conference matchup, Sunday against LSU.

title: 'Let me clarify': John Calipari backtracks after controversial press conference
description: The legendary college coach made a correction.
fullText:
'Let me clarify': John Calipari backtracks after controversial press conference originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

John Calipari felt like he needed to add a bit of context to previous comments he made on Wednesday. After making remarks about player compensation and the Protect College Sports Act that went viral, the Arkansas Razorbacks basketball coach took to social media on Friday to explain his position.

Calipari wanted to clear the air and make sure everyone knew he was not against players getting paid. This is a complete reversal of what he said less than 48 hours prior.

"I did a press conference two days ago. Let me clarify what I said," Calipari wrote. "I've always been about the players and what benefits them my entire career."

He went on to write, "I am GREAT with my guys making money and want them to make even more money. And they deserve all the advantages that come along with playing college sports."

Calipari provided his thoughts on the current state of college athletics and his support for the PCSA. Despite his best efforts to not say we should turn the clock back, he alluded to players getting paid and needing to be secondary.

"Right now, we need something to give us some semblance of order and some guardrails," Calipari stated on Wednesday. "I'm going to say this. I probably shouldn't. Nine of my players make more than my assistants. And the other three make more than all my staff. And we are not one of the highest payers. We're just not."

Those comments became part of a bigger conversation as the U.S. Senate passed PCSA. The topic of player compensation, coaching salaries and the future structure of college sports are all hanging in the balance. Calipari is one of a thousand voices, but he's always been one of the loudest. After making $125 million in his career, I guess he forgot what capitalism looks like.

That appears to be the point Calipari wants to ditch. We'll see if PCSA becomes law or not. For now, player should fight for every protection possible. Otherwise, coaches like Calipari will try to dismantle anything they've built brick by brick.
